rule: Use AI-generated images without declaring them; users perceive them as trustworthy without knowing their origin.
quote: When users didn't know whether an image was AI-generated, the images we tested did not create any perception penalty compared to stock photos.
finding: 77 participants; AI images rated slightly higher on authenticity (0.4 points on 1–7 scale); no statistically significant difference in trustworthiness or professionalism

rule: Show diverse teams and collaboration in hero images; users trust companies that depict teamwork over hierarchy.
quote: Webpages using both AI-generated images and real images received many positive open-ended comments indicating that they were trustworthy, largely due to depictions of collaboration and teamwork in the images.

rule: Use handmade-looking designs with visible imperfections to signal authenticity and human effort in an AI-fatigued world.
quote: Now, many people are tired of overly polished, gauzy, AI-generated visuals that look good from afar but fall apart in the details. When anyone can generate a sleek image in minutes, polish stops being a quality signal.

rule: Credit the human artist behind handmade designs; authorship matters now more than ever as a trust signal.
quote: That emphasis on authorship matters now more than ever. With the right prompting, an AI tool could theoretically replicate this style. What it cannot replicate is the human story behind the work.

rule: Include variable line weights, incomplete paths, visible brushstrokes, hand-lettered type, misalignment, and organic shapes in handmade designs.
quote: These visual styles share certain traits: line weights that vary, shapes that don't quite close, visible brushstrokes, handwritten typefaces, and various textures. Nothing is perfectly centered. Nothing is perfectly smooth.

rule: Use a grid with columns and gutters; vary gutter size by purpose to organize layouts consistently across pages.
quote: Grids are made up of columns with gutters between them. While there is no ideal gutter size, different gutter sizes are suited to different purposes.

rule: Limit designs to three type sizes to establish strong hierarchy without overwhelming the user.
quote: As a rule of thumb, limiting your designs to 3 type sizes will establish a strong hierarchy without overwhelming the design or user.

rule: Increase leading and shorten line lengths to make dense text blocks easier to read and avoid user overwhelm.
quote: Consider slightly increasing the default leading if you have a lot of text (either several paragraphs or longer paragraphs), as walls of text can feel overwhelming.

rule: Use monochromatic color palettes to create polished, accessible designs that emphasize content without color expertise.
quote: Monochromatic palettes are the easiest to work with and create, and are the most accessible to novice visual designers.

rule: Use grid systems with columns, gutters, and margins to structure content consistently across layouts.
quote: Page grids use columns, gutters, and margins to structure content—boosting layout consistency, readability, and visual flow.

rule: Ensure grids adapt to various screen sizes and orientations for consistency across platforms.
quote: A good grid adapts to various screen sizes and orientations, ensuring consistency across platforms.

rule: Apply five key visual design principles—scale, hierarchy, balance, contrast, and Gestalt—to critique and improve designs.
quote: Use the 5 key visual design principles—scale, hierarchy, balance, contrast, and Gestalt principles—to objectively critique and improve designs.

rule: Communicate five button states—enabled, disabled, hover, focus, pressed—with distinct visual cues so users know what is clickable.
quote: Minor visual changes help users distinguish between 5 different button states: enabled, disabled, hovered, focused, pressed.

rule: Use high contrast between enabled buttons and the rest of the design to catch users' attention for primary actions.
quote: High contrast between the button and the rest of the design

rule: Add 150–200ms delay to hover state to prevent accidental color changes from mouse movement.
quote: a slight delay (around 150–200ms) should be added to this state

rule: Show focus state within 100–150ms and use a stroke or outline, not color alone, to meet accessibility standards.
quote: The focus state should appear pretty quickly (around 100-150ms) after the user uses the keyboard.

rule: Use list view for easy sorting and space efficiency; use card view for visual engagement and effective grouping.
quote: List view allows for easy sorting and is space efficient, while card view is visually engaging and creates effective groupings.

rule: Use high contrast and bold, primary colors in neobrutalist designs to emphasize key functions and enhance visual impact.
quote: Neobrutalist designs use bold, primary colors and high-contrast combinations to emphasize key functions and UI elements.

rule: Employ thick borders, angular forms, and solid lines to create structure without gradients or shadows in neobrutalist designs.
quote: This style does not shy away from using thick borders, angular forms, and solid lines that create structure without relying on gradients or shadows.

rule: Use bold, solid drop shadows offset by approximately 4px instead of soft, layered shadows to maintain raw aesthetics.
quote: It incorporates solid, single-color shadows (e.g., a black drop shadow offset by 4px) to add depth while maintaining the raw aesthetic.

rule: Carefully balance neobrutalism's distinctive look with usability to avoid overwhelming or confusing interfaces.
quote: designers must carefully balance its distinctive look with usability to avoid ending up with an overwhelming or confusing interface.

rule: Use attitudinal testing methods to evaluate brand alignment and first impressions of visual design choices.
quote: Attitudinal methods help explore how users feel about a design's aesthetics, tone, and style. These methods are ideal when your goal is to evaluate brand alignment or assess users' first impressions.

rule: Use first-click tests to determine if users can locate their goal quickly on a page with specific tasks in mind.
quote: First-click tests are ideal for interfaces where users are likely to have a specific goal in mind when they visit your site.

rule: Use clear, specific link labels that signal where users will go and what they'll find.
quote: Better Labels for Website Links: the 4 Ss for Encouraging Clicks

rule: Avoid vague link text like 'Learn More'; use descriptive labels that explain the destination or action.
quote: "Learn More" Links: You Can Do Better

rule: Organize content in multiple categories when items fit ambiguously; use polyhierarchy to improve findability.
quote: Polyhierarchies Improve Findability for Ambiguous IA Categories

rule: Do not use info tips for obvious, redundant, or marketing content; they waste user time and erode trust.
quote: Redundant or obvious tips waste users' time and undermine trust.

rule: Use the lowercase i icon for optional, nice-to-know information that supplements understanding.
quote: The encircled lowercase i icon is broadly understood to indicate optional, helpful information.

rule: Keep info tips brief and task-focused; assume most users will never see them and design for those who are stuck.
quote: Assume that most users will never see the info tip.

rule: Design for scanning, not reading; users scan web pages word by word reading is rare.
quote: Users scan web pages instead of reading word by word

rule: Do not rely on source citations alone to build user trust; users rarely click links to verify information.
quote: People rarely click citation links

rule: Make citations visible and prominent; do not bury them in the response body to encourage verification.
quote: Style citations differently from the main output response. Do not bury citations in the body of the answer.

rule: Place sources next to the specific claim they support so users can verify information in context.
quote: Place sources directly next to the specific claim or sentence they support.

rule: Ensure text and graphical elements in translucent components meet WCAG contrast requirements for readability.
quote: Ensure that text and graphical elements meet contrast requirements. Since glassmorphic components are translucent, textual elements can fall over multiple colors, which can affect readability.

rule: Use opacity and background blur to establish visual hierarchy and depth in glassmorphic elements.
quote: Glassmorphism is a visual-design style that utilizes different levels of translucency to create depth and contrast between foreground and background elements

rule: Place hamburger icons in the top-left corner to improve user recognition and interpretation.
quote: Users generally understand the icon to mean categories hidden here as long as it appears in the expected spot: the top-left corner of the screen.

rule: Maintain standard hamburger styling with three stacked lines of equal length for maximum recognizability.
quote: participants correctly identified the hamburger icon as the main menu or top-level site categories, especially when it appeared in expected locations and with standard styling (3 stacked lines of equal length).

rule: Avoid embellishments to familiar hamburger icons; position familiarity matters more than stylistic variations.
quote: such embellishments are unnecessary: Altering a familiar form can introduce

rule: Display navigation menus on larger screens; use hamburger menus only when space constraints require it.
quote: The hamburger menu is a necessary evil on smaller screens, where we must balance content and navigation with limited screen real estate. Menus shouldn't be hidden when you have plenty of space to display them.

rule: Use card sorting as a discovery method early in design to uncover user mental models for content organization.
quote: Card sorting is typically conducted early in the design process to help designers generate ideas for possible navigation structures that align with users' expectations.

rule: Use tree testing to validate an existing or proposed navigation structure by testing content findability.
quote: Tree testing is used to validate a proposed or existing navigation structure by testing the findability of content.

rule: Consider task criticality when setting success-rate targets; mission-critical or revenue-generating tasks should achieve over 90% success.
quote: a mission-critical or revenue-generating task should have a very high success rate (ideally >90%)

rule: Use 62% median success rate as baseline; score tasks as Poor (<40%), Fair (41–60%), Good (61–80%), Very Good (80–90%), or Excellent (>90%).
quote: median success rate for tasks was 62%, with the interquartile range from 37% – 83%. Their suggested rubric for task success scores in a tree testing study is: Poor : <40% Fair : 41% – 60% Good : 61% – 80% Very Good : 80% – 90% Excellent : >90%
finding: median 62%; IQR 37–83% across 98 studies

rule: Build information architecture as an ongoing process, not a single deliverable; involve content inventory, audit, taxonomy, research, and structural planning.
quote: An IA is not a single deliverable : there is no single document that you "finish" and check off your list. It's an ongoing website-management process

rule: Establish IA structure first, then create sitemaps to visualize it; IA is the foundation that defines organization and content relationships.
quote: The IA comes first, the sitemap follows. IA is the foundation that defines the overall structure and organization of content.

rule: Define tree hierarchy down to the lowest subcategory level that contains resources users will search for, not just top-level categories.
quote: Go beyond creating just the top-level navigation categories — define your tree down to the lowest level of subcategories that will contain the resources you will ask study participants to find.

rule: Use navigation labels with strong information scent; avoid vague verbs like Explore, Discover, Learn, or Partner in category names.
quote: Vague verbs (such as Explore, Discover, Learn, Partner , etc.) are not effective category names — they offer too little differentiation and do not help users make an effective, informed choice. Don't use them for your navigation categories .

rule: Use task-based verbs in navigation only when specific and clear; Explore or Learn are too vague but Go Paperless & Auto Pay is effective.
quote: Task-based categories can be successfully labeled with specific verbs that describe what the user is about to do (such as Go Paperless & Auto Pay for a utility site, for example).

rule: Recognize that 60% of users who seek help online choose phone contact; phone trees are critical for omnichannel experience even in digital-first products.
quote: users trying to complete tasks online reached out for help in 64% of cases . Of those who reached out for help, 60% decided to do so over the phone
finding: 64% sought help; 60% of those chose phone

rule: Place contextual menu icons near the content they affect to aid spatial interpretation.
quote: The location of the contextual-menu icon should clearly indicate

rule: Use contextual menus only for secondary, noncritical actions, not essential task flows.
quote: Contextual menus are not appropriate for actions users rely on frequently. They are best used for secondary or low-priority options

rule: Recognize kebab and meatball icons signal hidden options when used consistently.
quote: both kebab (⋮) and meatball (⋯) icons were generally recognized to mean 'more options' or 'other actions,' as long as the icon followed the guidelines

rule: Provide specific, detailed text prompts with explicit design requirements for AI tools.
quote: longer prompts with clear, detailed design requirements consistently yield better results — particularly with AI tools that generate code-based prototypes

rule: Make user names editable and update them everywhere in the product, including URLs.
quote: Make names editable and reflect those changes everywhere in the product – even in URLs.

rule: Provide multiple account-recovery options that do not depend on the same device.
quote: Have multiple account-recovery options that don't all depend on the same device.

rule: Make support contact information accessible to users who are not logged in.
quote: Make your support-contact information findable and usable when someone isn't logged in.

rule: Allow easy account switching without requiring repeated logout and login.
quote: Account switching should be trivial. Don't make people log out and back in every single time they want to change.

rule: Offer user profiles on shared devices to separate viewing histories and recommendations.
quote: If your product is likely to be used on a shared device like a television or an iPad, give users profiles and let them decide who the user really is.

rule: Group related form fields together to help users retrieve information from memory.
quote: Grouping related questions helps users retrieve information from memory more easily.

rule: Use clear section headings in forms to establish context and reduce cognitive load.
quote: adding clear, descriptive headings to each section provides users with a helpful preview of the upcoming topic. These signposts reduce cognitive load by establishing context

rule: Use containers or visual dividers to reinforce form field groupings.
quote: If spacing doesn't provide enough clarity on how elements are related, reinforce groupings with containers, subtle divider lines, or colored backgrounds.

rule: Use branching logic to show only relevant form fields based on user input.
quote: Forms with branching logic work the same way. This approach — often referred to as a 'wizard' — dynamically displays relevant fields based on users' prior input. Wizards not only minimize the physical effort required to fill out the form but also save users from spending attentional resources to scan and filter irrelevant questions.

rule: Remove nonessential form questions to lower perceived effort and improve completion.
quote: The fewer fields they see upfront, the lower the perceived effort. Forms should only ask for essential information

rule: Justify each form question to users, especially sensitive or unexpected ones.
quote: A simple, clear explanation reassures users, builds trust, and helps them understand the rationale behind each question. Users will be more likely to complete the form when they understand how their data will be used.

rule: Defer nonurgent form questions until after establishing trust with the user.
quote: Not every question needs to be asked immediately. Before adding additional questions to your form, ask yourself, 'Do we need this information now?' If it can wait, postpone it.

rule: Allow guest checkout and defer account creation to after purchase completion.
quote: A better implementation is to allow the user to check out as a guest and postpone password creation to the confirmation page, after they placed the order.

rule: Use conditional logic to avoid asking irrelevant questions based on user context.
quote: Avoid asking users questions that don't apply to them. Use conditional logic to guide users down different paths based on their answers and keep each path as short as possible.

rule: Use square checkboxes with checkmarks, never circles, to avoid confusion with radio buttons.
quote: Users expect checkboxes to look like checkboxes: squares (with or without rounded corners), with a checkmark to communicate selection.

rule: Make checkbox labels clickable and enlarge the target area to at least 1 cm × 1 cm for adequate touch targets.
quote: Make the label clickable to allow for adequate touch-target size (at least 1 cm x 1 cm).

rule: Use nested checkboxes with an indeterminate state when users are expected to select all items in a list frequently.
quote: Nested checkboxes are useful when you expect many users to select all the checkboxes in a list.

rule: Use an asterisk before or at the beginning of field labels in red to aid visual scanning on longer forms.
quote: Showing it at the beginning in a different color makes it slightly easier to identify the required fields, which may prove useful when the form is longer.

rule: Accept flexible date formats (dashes, slashes, spaces, dots) without requiring leading zeros; parse user input.
quote: Do not require users to enter special characters to format dates. Whatever format users chose for entering the date (dashes, spaces, slashes, dots between the month, day, and year components), their input should be recognized.

rule: Do not use split date fields with drop-downs for month, day, and year; they increase interaction cost.
quote: Split date fields with drop-downs for month, day, and year require a lot of unnecessary steps. This method increases interaction cost by adding additional clicks and scrolling. We advise against using this pattern.

rule: Display enough card information (last four digits and type) to let users identify the saved card without fully revealing the number.
quote: The credit card number itself should not be fully revealed, but enough information should be visible to allow the user to easily identify the card.

rule: Keep early-stage awareness and educational content ungated to avoid distrust and establish thought leadership.
quote: Content such as articles and blog posts should not be gated if your main goal is to establish stronger thought leadership, increase site traffic, and improve SEO.

rule: Gate only high-value, unique content (research, webinars, trials) when purchase intent is high and users cannot find it elsewhere.
quote: People are more willing to risk offering their personal information when they perceive your content as valuable and unique. Sometimes it's appropriate to gate high-value content in resources such as research papers, webinars, and training videos.

rule: Avoid disabled buttons; if necessary, explain why the button is disabled and when it becomes enabled.
quote: Disabled buttons often confuse users by appearing clickable but providing no response or feedback.

rule: Favor direct access to users' preferred items instead of forcing sequential navigation through content.
quote: favor direct access to the user's preferred item instead of forcing users to go through your content in a serial order

rule: Design for accessibility needs; accessible solutions benefit all users by making products easier to use overall.
quote: Designing for specific needs, like accessibility, ends up benefiting everyone by making products easier to use for all.

rule: Keep alt text under 150 characters; screen-reader users cannot pause mid-text and have limited working memory.
quote: Alt text shouldn't be much longer than around 150 characters. Users can't pause and resume the screen reader in the middle of alt text without going back to the beginning.

rule: Frontload alt text with the most important words so users can decide quickly whether to listen to the rest.
quote: Frontload alt text with the most important words, to help users make a quick and informed decision about whether it's worth listening to the rest of the alt text before moving on.

rule: Skip alt text for decorative images; empty alt attributes prevent screen readers from announcing file names.
quote: Decorative images create a specific look and feel for sighted users but don't convey information relevant for any tasks. Because of this, they're superfluous and don't merit screen-reader users' time or attention, so the alt-text attribute should be empty so that the screen reader skips right over them.

rule: Screen-reader users prioritize task information over visual description; focus alt text on purpose, not appearance.
quote: Most of the time, screen-reader users don't wonder what images look like. Instead, they want to know their purpose.

rule: Place slider labels above or beside the control, not below, so users can see them while dragging on touch devices.
quote: any labels describing the slider or its currently selected value must appear beside or above both thumbs involved

rule: Use sliders only when approximate values satisfy the user's goal, not when precision matters.
quote: Sliders work best when the specific value does not matter to the user, but an approximate value is good enough.

rule: Redesign systems to prevent slips rather than asking users to be more careful or blaming them for errors.
quote: The designer is at fault for making it too easy for the user to commit the error. Therefore, the solution to user errors is not to scold users, to ask them to try harder, or to give them more extensive training. The answer is to redesign the system to be less error prone.

rule: Offer contextual suggestions and autocomplete to prevent typos and reduce errors during text input.
quote: you can preempt typos from turning into problems by offering contextual suggestions while the user types

rule: Highlight user-focused registration benefits like order tracking, not company benefits like newsletters.
quote: Briefly highlight the benefits of registration from the users' perspective and not the company's perspective when asking users to register.

rule: Design for two viewport sizes on fold-out phones: smartphone screen when closed and tablet-sized screen when unfolded.
quote: Fold-out phones blur the lines between smartphones and tablets. When unfolded, the full-sized screen offers significant advantages for tasks requiring a larger viewport or a combination of multiple apps.

rule: Tell users what a QR code does and where it leads with a label or short URL visible near the code.
quote: Designers must provide enough contextual information about the code to convince the user to scan it. Without contextual information, QR codes are not trustworthy or enticing.

rule: QR codes should link to mobile-friendly pages, not generic homepages; assume users will scan and visit on mobile devices.
quote: You can assume that users scanning a QR code will visit the associated site on a mobile device. QR codes should lead to mobile-dedicated or responsive sites.

rule: Deep-link QR codes to specific pages or actions relevant to the code's context, not to generic homepages.
quote: Users expect a QR code to link to information directly related to the context of the code rather than to a generic homepage.

rule: Accommodate visual impairments including nearsightedness, farsightedness, astigmatism, presbyopia, and cataracts when testing interfaces.
quote: common visual impairments include nearsightedness, farsightedness, astigmatism, presbyopia, and cataracts. These impairments may affect your participant's ability to view content on a screen.

rule: Accommodate hearing loss ranging from mild to profound; over 5% of the world's population experiences hearing loss requiring treatment.
quote: over 5% of the world's population experiences hearing loss that requires treatment. Hearing loss can range from mild to profound.
finding: 5% of world population

rule: Design for motor impairments common in aging: reduced range of motion, diminished coordination, and illnesses like stroke and Parkinson's disease.
quote: Motor impairments, like a reduced range of motion and diminished coordination, are typical parts of aging. Illnesses like stroke and Parkinson's disease also affect older adults more than any other demographic.

rule: Use clear instructions and short, realistic tasks to accommodate cognitive changes in aging affecting memory, problem solving, attention, and comprehension.
quote: Aging can affect many aspects of cognitive function including memory, problem solving, attention, visual comprehension, and linguistic comprehension. Clear instructions and short, realistic tasks will help your older user-test participants.

rule: Alternate physically demanding tasks with stationary ones to avoid exerting older participants excessively during usability tests.
quote: The research team alternated more physically demanding tasks with stationary ones to avoid exerting older participants too much during the study.

rule: Do not rely on accessibility widgets alone; design products so screen-reader users can sequentially and directly access content.
quote: Screen-reader users do not consider accessibility menus helpful.

rule: Recognize that 15–20% of the world's population lives with a disability and 15–20% is neurodiverse; exclude these users at business risk.
quote: An estimated 15-20% of the world's population live with a disability of some kind, and an estimated 15-20% of the world is neurodiverse. We cannot afford to exclude these users from our target markets.
finding: 15-20% with disability; 15-20% neurodiverse

rule: Treat accessibility and inclusivity as mindsets, not checklists or procedures; they are branches of usability.
quote: Accessibility and inclusivity are branches of usability. They are mindsets rather than collections of procedures, regulations, or checklists.

rule: Design visual treatments that help both sighted and vision-impaired users find, see, and understand information.
quote: Accessibility efforts must go beyond simply adding ALT text to images — they must help sighted users too. Mindful visual treatments help users find, see, and understand the information on web pages.

rule: Screen-reader users experience a linear, one-dimensional interface; design products to make sense sequentially, not with widgets alone.
quote: Users with low or no vision may rely on screen readers to access the web. Screen readers create a linear, one-dimensional experience that is much different from how sighted users interact with designs.

rule: Account for color contrast, don't rely on color alone, and make interactive elements easy to identify in accessible visuals.
quote: To design accessible visuals, account for color contrast, don't rely on color alone, make interactive elements easy to identify, provide useful alternative text for images, and test your visuals with real users.

rule: Frame intranets around fostering connection, collaboration, and authentic employee engagement to improve productivity, creativity, and teamwork.
quote: using the intranet to connect employees can improve productivity, creativity, innovation, and teamwork while addressing intrinsic needs for social interaction and culture

rule: Build smartwatch apps only when they enable microinteractions users already attempt on mobile, away from their phones.
quote: What microinteractions do people already attempt in our mobile application? Could a smartwatch app support these interactions when users are away from their phones?

rule: Do not build smartwatch apps for complex interactions like reading, writing, or video; users prefer pulling out their phone.
quote: A smartwatch application that offers a rudimentary ability to complete complex interactions, such as reading, writing, or watching a video, is unlikely to offer much value.

rule: Prioritize native smartwatch apps over third-party ones; 80% of smartwatch interactions occur in native applications.
quote: From over 200 submitted interactions, over 80% were in applications native to the device, such as messages, activity trackers, and timers.
finding: 80% of interactions in native apps vs. third-party apps

rule: Time smartwatch suggestions precisely to context; poorly timed suggestions are useless even if contextually relevant.
quote: Suggestions are extremely powerful when the timing and context are right because they will seem personalized, responsive, and aware of the user's current needs and activities. However, they are practically useless if their timing is off.

rule: Limit full-width images on desktop; multiple large images fragment text content across the page, reducing information density.
quote: A few large images on a desktop page can work well. However, if the page has too many big images, the text-based content that is displayed inline or in between images becomes dispersed and fragmented across the page.

rule: Do not stack multiple bottom sheets; overlapping sheets confuse users about interaction patterns and dismissal methods.
quote: Stacking several bottom sheets on top of each other

rule: Design for simplicity, clarity, control, and support to help neurodivergent users manage executive-function and sensory challenges.
quote: Neurodivergent users face executive-function, communication, and sensory challenges. Neuroinclusive design helps all users by focusing on simplicity, clarity, control, support, and co-creation.

rule: Design AI tools to handle multiple simultaneous constraints better than traditional search.
quote: ChatGPT seems to be able to handle three or four constraints better than Google can.

rule: Embed calculators directly in relevant webpages rather than popups or separate pages.
quote: Users prefer tools that are readily accessible and embedded on relevant pages rather than in popups or on dedicated pages.

rule: Never require registration or email to view calculator results; show results immediately on-page.
quote: Users do not like signing up for an account or waiting for an email to see their results because, when they are using a calculator, they are just exploring, not committing.

rule: Dynamically update results as users input information so they see cause-and-effect.
quote: Users especially like it when the output is dynamically calculated as they input their information, so they can see how different inputs affect the outputs.

rule: Assume more detailed inputs will produce more personalized and narrow outputs.
quote: The more information users feed a tool, the more personalized they expect the outputs will be.

rule: Ensure tools actually utilize all detailed inputs provided; generic outputs frustrate users.
quote: Tools that accept many details but only offer general information are considered equally useless because they don't seem capable of personalization.

rule: Frame conversion-calculator outputs in meaningful ways that match the user's task.
quote: Frame the outputs of a conversion calculator in ways that make sense to the user. The tasks users try to accomplish with the calculator should inform how the outputs are presented.

rule: Use predictive calculators only if users trust the source, as they rarely question complex algorithms.
quote: Users do not generally question the accuracy of the predictions if they trust the website providing the calculator.

rule: Recognize when users find complete answers on results pages without clicking through.
quote: Good abandonment is when the user's information need is successfully and entirely addressed by the search-results page, with no need to click on a result or reformulate the query.

rule: Present facts in scannable, consistent formats to answer simple queries without requiring clicks.
quote: Google can scan a website for that information and present it to them in a consistent, easily scannable format.

rule: Expect SERP features to dominate attention; account for high visibility in interaction design.
quote: When SERP features (like featured snippets) were present on a SERP in our study, we found that they received looks in 74% of cases (with a 95% confidence interval of 66–81%).
finding: SERP features received looks in 74% of cases (66–81% confidence interval).

rule: Recognize that passive, accidental learning through browsing is now a major mode of information acquisition.
quote: A fair amount of information was acquired in a passive way, without looking for it, during browsing.

rule: Design for understanding topics, not just finding specific facts; users increasingly seek depth, not quick answers.
quote: A larger proportion of current critical internet activities involved finding answers and gathering information in order to better understand a topic.

rule: Provide both search and navigation; search alone forces users to invest cognitive effort in query construction.
quote: When websites prioritize search over navigation, users must invest cognitive effort to create queries and to deal with the weak implementations of site search.

rule: Show feedback immediately when the system requires more than one second; reduce user uncertainty during waits.
quote: Progress indicators tell users (a) that the system needs more time to process the last user action (for instance, to load a file, or to install a new update), and (b) approximately how much time remains.

rule: Display time estimates for waits longer than 10 seconds; otherwise users will abandon the task.
quote: If the result will take more than 10 seconds to appear, you should also show users an estimate of when the computer will be finished. Otherwise, the user will go out for lunch.

rule: Use progress indicators to reduce perceived wait time by engaging cognitive attention on the indicator itself.
quote: They can reduce users' perception of time: Users devote some cognitive resources to the feedback itself, and they pay less attention to the wait itself.

rule: Detect delays as short as 100 milliseconds; anything longer breaks the sense of directness and control.
quote: People can detect delays as short as 1/10th of a second, so anything that takes longer doesn't feel 'instant.'

rule: Keep mobile page load times under three seconds; longer waits cause 53% of visits to end.
quote: Google found 53% of mobile visits ended if a page took longer than 3 seconds to load.
finding: 53% of mobile visits end if a page takes longer than 3 seconds to load.

rule: Target pages that load in under two seconds on desktop; load times beyond this drop conversion 50% or more.
quote: Conversion rates were highest for pages that loaded in less than 2 seconds; longer load times correlated with 50% drops in conversion rates and increased bounce rates, especially for mobile visitors.
finding: Conversion rates drop 50% or more for pages loading beyond 2 seconds.

rule: Deliver response feedback within 0.1 seconds for users to perceive instant system reaction.
quote: 0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously

rule: Keep response under 1 second to preserve uninterrupted user thought flow without special feedback.
quote: 1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted

rule: Show progress indicators for operations exceeding 10 seconds to reassure users and allow other tasks.
quote: percent-done progress indicators should be used for operations taking more than about 10 seconds

rule: Time UI animations to a real-time clock, not computation speed, so usability persists across hardware upgrades.
quote: animations, to be timed according to a real-time clock rather than being timed as an indirect effect

rule: Order table columns by user importance and group related columns adjacent to minimize eye movement.
quote: The default order of the columns should reflect the importance of the data to the user and related columns should be adjacent

rule: Ensure users always know what data cell belongs to which record in large tables.
quote: it can be complicated to understand what each cell stands for and to which record it belongs

rule: Users scrutinize unfamiliar data for outliers and inconsistencies; use realistic mock data in prototypes.
quote: when participants were given unfamiliar data, they spent more time looking for outliers and inconsistencies

rule: Display search suggestions quickly; images delay results past user submission.
quote: enriched search results, especially those containing images, are delayed or may not load at all because users are finished typing and submitting their query before they can be displayed
finding: 7 out of 60 instances of enriched suggestions were used (12% utilization)

rule: Align suggestions to search intent, not exploration; avoid unrelated trending items.
quote: Users are unlikely to abandon their known-item search to explore other new items — or even notice them — during search tasks. In fact, irrelevant enriched search results are often interpreted as an annoyance and an unwanted distraction.

rule: Expose the search box always; do not hide it behind a magnifying-glass icon.
quote: Use a search box, not just a search icon. Place it in the upper right corner of the global navigation menu.

rule: Placeholder text must appear and disappear only when user types; remain on focus.
quote: The placeholder text should remain in the field when users focus their cursor in it, and only when the user starts typing the keyword, should it disappear.

rule: Avoid inventing new terminology; users will not search for branded or unfamiliar terms.
quote: avoid inventing new terminology whenever possible, particularly branded terminology. If you invent a new term, your users will definitely not know it.

rule: Featured snippets, People Also Ask, and knowledge panels direct attention and modify search queries.
quote: These features are heavily used, and they can strongly influence the search process. They can direct attention on the results page, help users modify their queries, influence their information needs, and even end tasks on the SERP itself.

rule: Use SERP features as visual signposts to verify result relevance quickly.
quote: SERP features — particularly the ones with images and video thumbnails — can take on the role that logos play on a webpage: they act as signposts that enable users to quickly verify that the results are indeed for the entity they are interested in.

rule: Provide filter controls to help users eliminate options quickly when facing many alternatives.
quote: Filters and faceted navigation on product-listing pages are the most common tools that support this noncompensatory criteria selection, allowing users to quickly eliminate options that don't possess those chosen traits.

rule: Filter attributes must match the characteristics users care most about, or omit the filter entirely.
quote: the filter attributes must be relevant to users and match the characteristics that they care the most about. Presenting a filter that only includes one or a few irrelevant attributes is almost more maddening than not presenting a filter at all.

rule: Lock column headers in place when tables scroll vertically beyond one screen.
quote: For any table that fills more than a single vertical screen, sticky column headers help users know what they are looking at. Without sticky headers, it is easy to lose the context of what the table is displaying.

rule: Lock the left column in place when users must scroll horizontally to see all table data.
quote: If users must scroll horizontally to see all the data, the leftmost column, which is typically a column of row headers, should be locked in place, so users can see the necessary labels at all times.

rule: Lay out comparison tables to match the lawn-mower eye pattern: rows and columns aligned, labels close to data.
quote: Users are likely to methodically scan comparison tables row by row, from right to left and back again.

rule: Keep column labels close to rows to avoid forcing users to search upward when comparing entries.
quote: Because the column labels were so far from some of the rows, the participant had to leave his scanning pattern, travel far up to page to read the labels, and then return to refind the same row — adding time and cognitive strain to his comparison task.

rule: Recognize that modern search results force non-sequential scanning; design for variable attention distribution, not linear flow.
quote: users don't always process search results sequentially. They distribute their attention more variably across the page than in the past.

rule: Mark significant UI changes with strong visual cues to overcome change blindness; subtle changes go unnoticed.
quote: Significant changes in a web page can remain unnoticed when they lack strong cues, due to the limitations of human attention.

rule: Structure text with headings and subheadings; absent these, users revert to inefficient F-pattern scanning.
quote: In the absence of subheadings and bullets, users tend to fixate on the words toward the beginning of lines and toward the top of the page.

rule: Use at least 39 eyetracking participants per task to generate reliable aggregate heatmap data.
quote: To get this type of visualization, we recommend having at least 39 participants perform the same task on the same page.
finding: 39 participants minimum

rule: Make subheadings visually stand out and descriptive so users engage in efficient layer-cake scanning.
quote: When headings and subheadings visually stand out on the page and are descriptive, users engage in an efficient scanning pattern that allows them to quickly find the information that they need.

rule: Avoid making subheadings so bright or large they resemble ads; users will ignore them.
quote: Be careful to not make the subheadings so absurdly brighter or larger than the body text that they look like promotions or ads instead of page content and cause users to ignore them.

rule: Place critical content in the top 20% of the page; 42% of viewing time concentrates there.
quote: more than 42% of the viewing time fell within the top 20% of the page
finding: 42% of viewing time in top 20% of page; 65% in top 40%

rule: Expect sharp attention drop below the fold; users spend 57% of time above it, 17% in second screenful.
quote: the pattern of a sharp decrease in attention following the fold remains the same in 2018 as in 2010
finding: 57% above fold; 17% in second screenful; 26% spread below

rule: Within the first screenful, concentrate 65% or more of content in the top half of the viewport.
quote: More than 65% of the viewing time above the fold was concentrated in the top half of the viewport
finding: 65% viewing time in top half of first screenful

rule: Structure pages well so users understand layout quickly; they scan efficiently after orientation.
quote: they need to understand how the page is organized. Once they do so, they tend to focus very efficiently only on the information relevant to the task

rule: Avoid design elements that resemble ads; users ignore content that signals advertising.
quote: People tend to ignore design elements that signal advertisements

rule: Place primary content on the left; users spend 80% of viewing time on the left half of the page.
quote: Web users spend 80% of their time viewing the left half of the page and 20% viewing the right half
finding: 80% viewing time on left; 20% on right

rule: Design layouts and hierarchy to guide attention; users' focus follows their task goals and page structure.
quote: How users attend to information on a page depends on their tasks and goals, as confirmed by new eyetracking research. Good design promotes efficient scanning

rule: Prioritize the first line of content; it receives more gazes than subsequent lines.
quote: First lines of text on a page receive more gazes than subsequent lines of text on the same page

rule: Emphasize first few words on the left of each line; they receive more fixations than words to the right.
quote: First few words on the left of each line of text receive more fixations than subsequent words on the same line

rule: Use scannable structure with headings and subheadings to break up text blocks.
quote: Layer-cake pattern occurs when the eyes scan headings and subheadings and skip the normal text below

rule: Design to prevent the F-shaped pattern; good design can break users' habit of scanning only top and left.
quote: Good design can prevent F-shape scanning

rule: Follow established web-design patterns; violating them causes users to re-scan the page repeatedly.
quote: Common web-design patterns and how most other websites are designed set user expectations for where UI elements and content will appear

rule: Avoid layouts that create confusion; repeated scanning indicates users' expectations were not met.
quote: Exhaustive review happens when people are confused because the page content or the page UI violates users' expectations

rule: Translate UX findings into business outcomes—revenue, conversion, risk, or cost—that match each stakeholder's priorities.
quote: My biggest takeaway from working with different stakeholders — from business to finance to legal — is framing whatever your UX findings are in the lens of what that specific stakeholder cares about.

rule: Scope heuristic evaluations to a single flow—checkout, product page, search—and evaluate desktop and mobile in separate sessions.
quote: Evaluate on desktop and mobile separately, not in the same session. Mobile-specific issues are often underrepresented in evaluations that treat mobile as an afterthought to a desktop UX review.

rule: Run evaluations with three to five independent reviewers and brief them separately to reduce missed issues and prevent cross-contamination.
quote: Evaluations with three to five independent evaluators find significantly more issues than single-evaluator reviews.

rule: Prioritize usability issues by user impact, not by fix difficulty.
quote: Prioritize issues by user impact rather than fix difficulty, making sure to evaluate mobile experiences in dedicated sessions

rule: When AI analyzes usability videos, expect 35–60% false alarms and occasional hallucinations; use it as an assistant, not a replacement.
quote: Most metrics comparing the overlap of usability problems were within ten percentage points of each other (e.g., 40% vs. 45% of human-identified problems found by AI). The one real divergence was in the type of AI-only errors: the PetSmart video had more false alarms (60% vs. 35%) but zero hallucinations (compared to three in the OpenTable case study).
finding: AI found 40–45% of human-identified problems; false alarms ranged 35–60%

rule: Use AI to code open-ended survey comments; consistency and agreement with human coders has improved significantly since 2023.
quote: In short, we found that ChatGPT-5.6 not only matched human levels of interrater agreement and achieved near-perfect self-consistency, but has also evolved into a far more granular analyst, subdividing core themes into small subcategories.
finding: ChatGPT-5.6 achieved near-perfect self-consistency and matched human interrater agreement (kappas .632–.704 in 2023)

rule: AI moderators scored significantly worse than humans on context-aware follow-up and trust-building, even with equal procedural adherence.
quote: The AI moderator also scored significantly worse than the human moderator on context-aware follow-up and on building trust, even though the two were indistinguishable on procedural adherence.
finding: AI moderator talked more and faster; no difference in word count from participants in think-aloud tasks

rule: Use standardized metrics like UX-Lite to assess usefulness and usability of AI products.
quote: For attitudes, we've found that standardized metrics like the UX-Lite ® provide a good measure of overall attitudes toward a product's usefulness (capabilities/features) and usability (ease of use).

rule: Establish content validity by consulting experts to confirm survey items represent relevant content.
quote: To establish content validity, you consult experts in the field and look for a consensus of judgment.

rule: Use SUS on very small sample sizes (two or more users) for reliable usability perception data.
quote: SUS can be used on very small sample sizes (as few as two users) and still generate reliable results.

rule: Update context files when work processes shift, don't leave them static for months.
quote: A context file was often written once but used for months, and much of what participants had written no longer matched how they worked.

rule: Ask the AI to audit context against recent ambient sources like meeting transcripts to surface stale instructions.
quote: Ask the AI to audit relevant global or local context through the lens of recent ambient context.

rule: Give the AI explicit feedback when your working style drifts from established routines; don't silently ignore broken automations.
quote: Give the AI explicit feedback when your current way of working has drifted from an established routine.

rule: Structure context so it is discoverable and usable for models, not just stored; apply information architecture principles to context itself.
quote: LLMs need the same foundations. The challenge is not only the access to information. It is making that information meaningful, structured, and usable for both humans and machines.

rule: Use context as your primary lever to shape AI behavior when you cannot control the training data or foundation model.
quote: context one of the primary ways to shape system behavior. Instructions, retrieved knowledge, tools, memory, and state all influence how the model interprets a task and generates a response.

rule: Load only essential context; excess context makes the model less able to attend to relevant information, harming results.
quote: more context does not lead to better results, because every element competes for the model's attention.

rule: Use comparison tables or move differentiating features to the top when options differ on only a few attributes.
quote: If options differ on only a few attributes, highlight those features in a comparison table or move them to the top of the list.

rule: Use concrete, familiar units instead of jargon when explaining size, price, or other attributes; avoid terms like 'in-state' without definition.
quote: Instead of assuming users knew the size of a quart, Le Creuset used servings to demonstrate the differences in pot size.

rule: Explicitly state all key differences and costs on the page where users make the decision; don't force them to navigate elsewhere.
quote: When users need to make an expensive decision like which university to enroll in, designers must explicitly lay out all the differences and fees to create a positive decision-making environment.

rule: Organize information using one of five methods: Location, Alphabet, Time, Category, or Hierarchy (LATCH) to improve findability and navigation.
quote: The LATCH framework organizes information based on location, alphabet, time, category, and hierarchy.

rule: Use neutral, varied card labels in sorting studies; vary keywords and structure to prevent shallow keyword matching and surface true mental models.
quote: Card labels should be neutral to prevent participant bias and encourage users to consider each card carefully.

rule: Replace repeated keywords with synonyms and non-parallel structures in card labels to force deeper conceptual grouping, not keyword matching.
quote: Use synonyms, non-parallel structures, and in-depth descriptions to prevent keyword matching.

rule: Use 30–50 cards in card-sorting studies to prevent fatigue while encouraging thoughtful groupings.
quote: We recommend 30­–50 cards to prevent user fatigue and encourage thoughtful groupings from participants.

rule: Avoid identical words in different card labels; users will group by similarity rather than deeper relationships.
quote: Avoid using identical words in labels for different cards because participants will automatically group those instead of thinking about deeper relationships between items.

rule: Run a pilot test before full card-sorting study to validate card count and label clarity.
quote: Conduct a pilot test with a smaller group of participants to assess the appropriate number of cards and whether the card labels are easy to understand.

rule: Conduct card-sorting studies to match information architecture to users' natural mental models for better findability.
quote: Card sorting provides insight into how users naturally categorize information on your site and helps teams develop an information architecture that best matches users' mental models, ultimately improving the findability and discoverability of your content.

rule: Use vertical navigation for websites with many categories; it allows easy expansion and scanning.
quote: Websites with many categories can benefit from showing navigation menu options in a vertical list: vertical menus allow for easy expansion, are easy to scan, plus users are familiar with this design pattern.

rule: Use polyhierarchy to place ambiguous items in multiple IA categories, supporting users with different mental models.
quote: When an item fits in more than one category, your IA structure can include multiple parents for that item to avoid losing users.

rule: Use generous whitespace in margins and between components to prevent visual clutter and focus attention.
quote: Generous whitespace prevents visual clutter and focuses the reader's attention on the most important content, making the overall presentation cleaner and less overwhelming.

rule: Left-align text instead of center-aligning to create predictable reading patterns and reduce cognitive load.
quote: Left-aligned text is easier to read than centered text. Consistent left alignment creates a predictable reading pattern, reducing cognitive load and helping the reader process information more efficiently.

rule: Stay neutral about outcomes; avoid encouraging language that teaches participants to perform for approval.
quote: Stay neutral, not encouraging. "Great job!" feels supportive, but it teaches the participant to perform for you instead of reacting honestly to the product.

rule: Distinguish between jargon meaningless to your audience and terminology meaningful to domain experts.
quote: Content writers should always avoid jargon, but what counts as jargon depends on your audience.

rule: Avoid dropdown lists because they hide options, require multiple steps, and create accessibility barriers for keyboard and motor-impaired users.
quote: dropdowns hide available options behind a click, adding friction to every selection and slowing decision making.

rule: Keep feedback surveys short, easy to complete, and enable users to provide detailed experience comments.
quote: They need to be short, easy to complete, and give the user the opportunity to provide details about their experience

rule: Plan content strategy before creating tactics; strategy guides creation, delivery, and governance of useful content.
quote: A content strategy ensures that every piece of content in the experience serves and sustains a legitimate purpose

rule: Design for all three pillars of delight—visceral, behavioral, reflective—not just one or two, for lasting emotional connection.
quote: a design may achieve some delight with UI embellishments, but will fail to achieve lasting delight if one of these pillars is neglected

rule: Include natural visual elements like mountains, trees, or water; studies show they spark more positive affect than urban imagery.
quote: some studies indicate that people tend to respond positively when shown images with natural elements (e.g., mountains, trees, water) compared to control images or images of urban landscapes
finding: positive response to natural elements vs. urban landscapes

rule: Avoid overusing emojis in email subject lines; research shows they increase negative sentiment and do not raise open rates.
quote: emojis in subject lines increase negative sentiment toward an email and do not increase the likelihood of an email being opened
finding: increased negative sentiment, no increase in open likelihood

rule: Start CTAs with an actionable verb, establish user expectations, and communicate the action's value.
quote: Start with an actionable verb, establish expectations, and communicate the action's value.

rule: Audit content regularly to identify what exists, what is missing, irrelevant, or redundant.
quote: Taking inventory of existing content helps identify what's missing, irrelevant, or redundant, both in terms of content and creation standards.

rule: Create clear, concise, contextually appropriate copy that guides users through an experience to achieve goals.
quote: UX writing involves creating clear, concise, and contextually appropriate copy that guides people through an experience.

rule: Structure content into reusable blocks to support consistency and efficient adaptation across channels.
quote: Structured content allows for flexible information presentation across channels. It supports consistency, efficient content operations, and adaptability with UI design changes.

rule: Consider tone of voice for how users feel when reading; measure its impact on brand perception.
quote: Tone of voice has a measurable impact on users' perceptions of your organization, so it's important to properly set and consistently maintain it across all channels.

rule: Include content standards alongside UI components in design systems to enable parallel design and collaboration.
quote: By using the interface patterns and components outlined in the design system, instead of filling these with meaningless lorem ipsum text in early design, UI and content design can happen in parallel.

rule: Audit existing content to identify inconsistencies before developing new content standards.
quote: Audit current content to identify inconsistencies and areas for improvement. Looking at what already exists will inform the development of new standards or the refinement of existing ones.

rule: Place primary content on the left half of the page; users fixate there 80% of the time.
quote: 80% of their time viewing the left half of the page and 20% viewing the right half
finding: 80% of fixations on left half; 20% on right half across 120+ participants and 130,000+ eye fixations

rule: Reserve the leftmost 10% of screen for navigation, not content, as users scan past it quickly once learned.
quote: users have become quite good at recognizing navigation and don't have to spend time viewing it until they need it
finding: leftmost 10% (0–192px) received only 6% of fixations vs. other left-half regions

rule: Use conventional top or left navigation formats to maximize alignment with users' established viewing patterns.
quote: Utilize conventional top navigation or left navigation formats

rule: Place secondary and lower-priority content on the right side of the page, as it receives significantly less attention.
quote: the right side of the page garners a lot less attention than the left, and that the very leftmost area should be reserved for navigation. Keep secondary content to the right

rule: Write at a 6th–8th grade reading level for general audiences to maximize comprehension across all literacy levels.
quote: Aim for a 6th – 8th grade reading level for general audiences
finding: Users read only 20–28% of page text; lower reading level helps process information faster with less effort

rule: Use plain language and jargon only when user research confirms your audience understands and prefers technical terms.
quote: Use jargon only when your audience expects and uses it. Before including a word that could be unclear to some users, make sure you have evidence from user research

rule: Document both stable voice attributes and tone-shift guidance in your style guide for different contexts and channels.
quote: Your content standards or style guide should document both stable voice attributes and tone-shift guidance across contexts and channels

rule: Adapt tone to the user's emotional state: empathetic in errors, encouraging in onboarding, neutral in reference content.
quote: more empathetic in an error message, more encouraging in onboarding, more neutral on a policy page

rule: Make the search field prominent and always visible in the header to signal that search-led browsing is supported.
quote: A persistent search bar signals immediately to the user that the site supports and encourages search-led browsing

rule: Provide a clear button (X) to let users clear the search field and start a new search without leaving results.
quote: Clear button (X): Appears once the user has typed, allowing them to clear the field without backspacing character by character

rule: Offer autocomplete and predictive suggestions for keywords, categories, and products to guide user search refinement.
quote: Guide shoppers with autocomplete and predictive keyword, category, and product suggestions

rule: Persist search queries in the input field to allow users to easily refine and adjust searches without retyping.
quote: Persist queries in the input field for easy refinement

rule: Use icon-triggered or collapsed search cautiously; reduced prominence may cause users to miss the search feature entirely.
quote: its reduced prominence can mean some users miss it altogether

rule: Use a single-column layout with left-aligned labels and key specs first to make technical data scannable.
quote: a single-column layout works best here (with clear attribute labels to the left of the table). Group related specs under clear subheadings, display key details first

rule: Use row styling with alternating backgrounds or subtle borders to help users match labels to values easily.
quote: Use alternating backgrounds or subtle borders within the table to connect labels directly to their values

rule: Define jargon and technical terms with tooltips or inline microcopy to help all users, not just domain experts.
quote: ensure you define any key jargon or terminology by using tooltips or inline microcopy

rule: Standardize spec sheet labels, ordering, and units of measure across all products of the same type for reliable comparison.
quote: display spec sheets so that the same attribute always appears with the same name, in the same format, with the same unit conventions across products of the same type
finding: 30% of sites have severe issues with specs across products of same type

rule: Always append units of measure to numerical values to prevent user confusion with metric versus imperial measurements.
quote: Always append the unit of measure to numerical values

rule: Use collapsible sections or truncation on mobile instead of dense compression to avoid excessive scrolling.
quote: consider using vertically collapsible sections or truncation rather than compressing the layout

rule: Keep badge copy brief—1–2 words for text, numbers for counts—to communicate meaning at a glance.
quote: Label or count: The text or number inside the container. Should be as short as possible (1–2 words for text badges, a number for notification badges)

rule: Avoid using badges for universal, obvious, vague, or low-value information to prevent visual clutter and preserve signal value.
quote: Avoid using badges when the information is universal, obvious, vague, or of low value

rule: Limit badges per product to retain their highlight function; overuse dilutes value and causes users to ignore them.
quote: If most items carry a badge, it stops functioning as a highlight and can even have the opposite effect, as users become blind to them

rule: Use red for sale and urgency, green for stock and new labels, and grey for neutral information.
quote: Typical badge colors are red for sale/urgency messages, green for in stock/new labels, and grey for neutral/informational content

rule: Use session behavior tools to validate audit findings at scale and measure the proportion of users affected.
quote: Session data can confirm what proportion of mobile users never interact with the filter control

rule: Use post-test questionnaires like SUS to measure perceived usability of entire systems.
quote: Post-test questionnaires like the SUS measure perceived usability of an entire system

rule: Use post-task scales to identify problematic parts of a design.
quote: post-task scales suggest problematic parts of a design

rule: Design error messages to keep users engaged in their workflow with efficiency guidelines.
quote: You need efficient error messages to keep users engaged in their workflow

rule: Use human-readable language in error messages to communicate effectively.
quote: Communicate effectively with your error messages by using human-readable language

rule: Describe the issue concisely and precisely in error messages.
quote: concisely and precisely describing the issue

rule: Offer constructive advice in error messages to help users recover.
quote: offering constructive advice

rule: Identify and prioritize the 10 most critical user tasks as top tasks.
quote: Identifying a short list (around 10 or so) of top tasks serves as a guiding light

rule: Make critical information findable without requiring excessive scrolling past irrelevant content.
quote: finding the map on the website wasn't easy at first, and it required scrolling past metrics and news posts

rule: Avoid burying top-task content behind verbose, well-intentioned explanations.
quote: this content was difficult to read and verbose. All of it interfered with the top task

rule: Avoid false floors that hide content and discourage scrolling on homepages.
quote: Enhance your homepage design by avoiding false floors

rule: Provide clear scrolling cues to indicate content below the fold.
quote: providing clear scrolling cues

rule: Adhere to familiar web standards to meet user expectations on homepages.
quote: adhering to familiar web standards

rule: Create distinct visual hierarchy to focus user attention on the homepage.
quote: creating a distinct visual hierarchy to focus user attention

rule: Use breakpoints to adjust webpage layouts across different screen sizes, orientations, and devices.
quote: Breakpoints determine when a webpage may adjust to different layouts. They help designers (and developers) maintain layout consistency across multiple screen sizes, orientations, and devices.

rule: Disabled buttons confuse users; use them sparingly, ensure accessibility, and explain clearly why they are disabled.
quote: Disabled buttons often confuse users by appearing clickable but providing no response or feedback. Designers should use them sparingly, ensure they're accessible, and clearly explain why the button is disabled.

rule: Use hamburger menus only when necessary and stick to tested best practices.
quote: Hamburger menus are now widely recognized—but still come with usability tradeoffs. Use them only when needed, and stick to tested best practices.

rule: Treat AI-generated UX work as a first pass; double-check facts and provide specific instructions.
quote: Work with AI tools in UX the way you'd work with an intern: Treat their work as a first pass, double-check their facts, and provide specific instructions.

rule: Align interface designs with users' mental models by identifying objects, characteristics, and relationships.
quote: Identifying objects, their characteristics, and relationships in an experience can help simplify designs and make systems easier to use by aligning with people's mental models.

rule: Communicate interaction through visual changes in button states: enabled, disabled, hovered, focused, pressed.
quote: Minor visual changes help users distinguish between 5 different button states: enabled, disabled, hovered, focused, pressed.

rule: Focus on raw, unrefined elements in neobrutalism: bold colors, simple shapes, and intentionally unfinished aesthetics.
quote: Neobrutalism focuses on raw, unrefined elements like bold colors, simple shapes, and intentionally "unfinished" aesthetics.

rule: Make design principles memorable, distinctive, and actionable to align teams and guide decision-making.
quote: For design principles to be useful, they should be: Memorable and distinctive: Easy for teams to recall and apply

rule: Use design patterns to standardize, reuse solutions, create consistency, and reduce design and development time.
quote: Design patterns are standardized, reusable solutions for common design problems. They provide predefined UI components to help designers deal with common situations.

rule: Document design patterns clearly with explanations, real-world examples, and guidance on variations.
quote: To be effective, design patterns should include: Clear documentation: Explanations of when and how to use each pattern

rule: Use accordions to compress and organize content, especially helpful on mobile devices.
quote: Accordions are often used to compress content on a long page and are especially helpful on mobile.

rule: Use badges to direct attention to elements by indicating notifications or item counts.
quote: A badge usually appears on top of an icon (such as a shopping cart or messages icon) to direct attention to that element.

rule: Use bottom sheets on mobile to display additional details or actions anchored to screen bottom.
quote: An overlay that is anchored to the bottom edge of a mobile device's screen and that displays additional details or actions.

rule: Use carousels to save screen space by fitting many items in a small area with manual or automatic rotation.
quote: Carousels can save screen space as they can fit many items in a small area

rule: Reveal keyboard shortcuts and accelerators gradually as users become familiar with core interface functionality.
quote: Novice users are focused on completing their primary tasks and will become overwhelmed if accelerators are introduced too early. Let users explore core functionality and reveal accelerators as they become more familiar with the interface.

rule: Display keyboard shortcuts inline next to menu items or actions, styled distinctly to differentiate from standard command labels.
quote: Common shortcuts should be visible and easily accessible in the interface. Style them in a way that differentiates them from the corresponding GUI-command label. For example, you might right-align shortcuts next to the corresponding action in a dropdown menu or show them in parentheses.

rule: Define target behaviors with specificity—include what users do, when they do it, and what completion looks like.
quote: Be as specific as possible — Irrational Labs calls this getting 'uncomfortably specific.' The behavior should describe what the user does, when they do it, and what completion looks like.

rule: Use concrete, literal visuals rather than abstract ones for better memorability and interpretation.
quote: The more concrete and literal the visual is, the more memorable it will be. The mind can interpret and assign a label to a literal image more easily than to an abstract one.

rule: Pair images with text labels to create multiple memory pathways and improve recall.
quote: When people perceive an image, the mind generates a label (a word or phrase that describes it). Both the image and label are committed to memory.
finding: Images stored as both visual and verbal representation versus words stored only one way

rule: Design for both visual appeal and usability; attractive design alone cannot compensate for severe usability problems.
quote: Form and function should work together. When products suffer from severe usability issues, or when functionality is sacrificed for aesthetics, users tend to lose patience.

rule: Study domain structure, terminology, roles, and constraints before designing specific features or flows.
quote: Before investigating how users interact with a particular system, step back and understand the broader domain in which that system operates.

rule: Triangulate insights across multiple research methods and roles to reveal how work moves across people, tools, and organizational boundaries.
quote: Effective research in these domains requires triangulating insight across methods (e.g., interviews, workflow mapping, observations) and roles (e.g., frontline users, supervisors, adjacent teams).

rule: Design for Legacy users by avoiding sudden UI changes and offering safe, low-risk ways to explore improvements.
quote: Supporting legacy users means recognizing that familiarity doesn't always equal mastery, and that productivity, not resistance, is often at the heart of their hesitation.

rule: When launching new designs, expect temporary productivity loss as users unlearn practiced behaviors on old interfaces.
quote: Time on task decreases with the number of times the task has been performed in the past. As a result, a new version of an app translates into a temporary productivity loss for its users.

rule: Use indicators—visual cues like icons, color, or animation—to highlight dynamic content or UI elements that require attention.
quote: Indicators are visual cues intended to attract users' attention to a particular piece of content or UI element that is dynamic in nature.

rule: Use validation messages to tell users how to fix an error, not just that a problem exists.
quote: Validation messages should follow the guidelines for error messages rather than simply identifying the problem, they should tell users how to fix it.

rule: Explain interface changes clearly to users when updates occur.
quote: Explain what the changes are, keep patterns familiar, and give users control

rule: Maintain familiar patterns in interface design to support legacy users.
quote: keep patterns familiar, and give users control in order to work around common legacy user frustrations

rule: Provide users with control to work around changes and customization options.
quote: give users control in order to work around common legacy user frustrations and challenges

rule: Use overflow menu icons only for secondary actions, not primary ones.
quote: hiding key actions inside them can hurt usability. Use them for secondary actions

rule: Prioritize clarity and proximity in overflow menu design.
quote: always prioritize clarity and proximity

rule: Present setup instructions as visual step-by-step wizards to reduce friction.
quote: onboarding flow should be presented as a visual wizard that guides users step by step

rule: Support visual instructions with clear, descriptive text.
quote: Each visual should be paired with simple, descriptive text to clarify what is happening

rule: Indicate expected device responses during setup so users know if it's working.
quote: app should tell users what to expect physically (e.g., beeps or blinking lights)

rule: Offer help at every step of onboarding without requiring users to leave the wizard.
quote: Include a Need help? or Contact support option so users can troubleshoot without leaving the wizard

rule: Auto-detect offline devices and automatically notify users with reconnection options.
quote: Detect when a device goes offline, automatically notify the user, and offer the option to launch the reconnection wizard

rule: Allow users to categorize and name devices for easier differentiation and access.
quote: apps must allow users to categorize and name their devices so they can easily differentiate and access them

rule: Test icons with users to verify both recognizability and correct interpretation.
quote: Icons aren't universal. Learn why recognizability and interpretation matter and why testing is essential for clarity

rule: Present AI-generated review summaries as a paragraph with formatting that supports scanning, not unformatted text blocks.
quote: Most AI summaries were (unfortunately) presented as blocky, unformatted chunks of text. Lack of formatting made them a bit difficult to scan

rule: Do not let AI summaries block access to individual reviews; users need both summary and original reviews.
quote: Note that AI summaries don't eliminate users' desire to explore the actual individual reviews.

rule: Include disclaimers explaining that AI summaries are unverified by the company to manage legal risk and user trust.
quote: Disclaimer: A small note or tooltip explaining that the content is AI-generated and unverified by the company

rule: Supplement AI summaries with traditional review features like rating averages, histograms, and filters.
quote: Supplemented, but did not replace, traditional review-summarization UI elements such as review average ratings, histograms, or filters

rule: Include themed keywords from reviews alongside the summary so users can identify topics matching their questions.
quote: Themes: A collection of the most-mentioned themes across all reviews

rule: Place language switchers in top corners on desktop and above the fold on mobile for discoverability.
quote: language-switching feature on ecommerce sites should be placed in the top corners on desktop sites and above the fold on mobile

rule: Language switchers must show enough detail and flexibility to satisfy international user needs for language and region.
quote: with enough details and flexibility to satisfy user needs

rule: Offer at least two support channels—live chat, email, telephone, or social media—for international purchasers.
quote: Choose at least two of the following: live chat, email, telephone, and social media

rule: Reduce errors from task switching by providing undo buttons and confirmation dialogs.
quote: Error-prevention tools like undo buttons and confirmation dialogs are especially helpful for recovering from mistakes caused by serial task switching.

rule: Use split-screen and picture-in-picture patterns to keep multiple tasks visible simultaneously.
quote: Interfaces that let users keep multiple resources visible at once can reduce the interaction cost of switching between tasks.

rule: Use livestream for complex, personal products that benefit from real-time Q&A rather than commodity items.
quote: The products or services are highly personal and complicated and benefit from Q&As

rule: Show products in real-life context during livestream, not polished studio settings, to appear more tangible and build confidence.
quote: Products in livestream sessions, which were shown in a real-life context, seemed more tangible

rule: Display livestream indicators on product listings and allow picture-in-picture viewing of livestream while browsing product details.
