quote: a livestreaming indicator appears on the product-listing page for those items with an ongoing livestream

rule: Write concise, easy-to-digest transactional messages; verbose content damages user trust in your brand.
quote: A concise message conveys the message that the customers' time is valued and, thus, helps increase trust in your brand

rule: Display diverse models across ecommerce site photography to help shoppers see themselves represented in products.
quote: When models were diverse, shoppers noticed. Many study participants were happy to see models of different sizes, ages, and races on ecommerce sites

rule: Allow shoppers to select models by size or height to visualize product fit on bodies similar to their own.
quote: Several of these sites went beyond just showing diverse models in site photography — they allowed shoppers to choose the model on which to view the products

rule: Provide detailed product information even when items cannot be purchased online to maintain customer interest.
quote: regardless of how much luxury brands want to sell online, they must provide better product details

rule: Support in-person visits by providing rich online product information even for items sold offline, because luxury shoppers research before purchasing in stores.
quote: even brands who don't want to allow online purchases still need ecommerce sites — just ones that lack a checkout process. This is because luxury shoppers often want to research products online, even when they intend to purchase them in person

rule: Design for the consideration phase of the luxury shopping journey, where brands often fail their customers.
quote: Luxury brands often fail their customers during the "consider" phase of their journey

rule: Show users which sources were searched and explain gaps when an AI agent cannot find information across multiple apps.
quote: An agentic experience must show the user which sources were searched and explain relevant gaps

rule: Design AI assistants to access and use relevant personal context already stored on users' devices without requiring manual data entry.
quote: An AI agent should answer questions about information that is already on the user's phone without making them find it and paste it into the conversation

rule: Plan AI system architecture for long-term durability and maintainability, not just short-term functionality.
quote: A big ball of mud is a system scraped together for short-term functionality, not architected for long-term durability

rule: Prioritize rebuilding and refactoring context and workflows instead of allowing throwaway code to accumulate and block future improvements.
quote: These throwaway pieces are rarely useless, so they stay. Participants seemed to have two reasons for not having the AI rebuild them: a lack of time and fear of breaking the existing value

rule: Disclose the specific role AI played and the extent of AI involvement, not just that AI was used, because audience reactions depend on both factors.
quote: audiences' reactions depend on knowing not only whether the AI was used, but also on knowing what role it played and how much AI contributed to the content

rule: Emphasize human judgment and accountability in AI disclosures, especially when human oversight is expected by the audience.
quote: readers had more negative reactions when the disclosure suggested that AI had produced the content autonomously, without clear human involvement and accountability

rule: Define success hotspots on interfaces and code clicks within them as success or failure to measure task completion.
quote: Certain hotspots/AOIs can be defined as part of an optimal 'happy' path, generally considered 'correct' in completing a task.

rule: Include your team in user research sessions so they experience stories firsthand, not secondhand through reports.
quote: Teams that observe user research are more likely to build a shared understanding and empathy for their users and the problem space.

rule: Present research findings as stories about user experiences, not just data themes, because stories engage memory and emotion more powerfully.
quote: Personal narratives engage brain regions associated with emotion, memory, and social reasoning more strongly than nonnarrative text.
finding: fMRI study showed personal narratives triggered widespread brain activity across listeners, including regions for social reasoning, emotional processing, and memory, versus only auditory or language regions for technical manual excerpts.

rule: Allow users to escalate immediately to a human agent when they explicitly request it, without gatekeeping or additional explanations.
quote: Never gatekeep when the user explicitly asks to be connected to a human. If a customer asks for a human agent, the bot should immediately honor that request.

rule: Design chatbots to handle questions adjacent to their trained domain, not just exact FAQs, so users feel the bot understands their real goals.
quote: A bot that's too narrow is rigid and misses questions adjacent to the user's goal; a bot that's too broad answers off-domain and drifts beyond what the company authorized. The target is the middle — appropriately scoped: flexible enough to handle adjacent questions, disciplined enough to redirect what's genuinely out of scope.

rule: Offer chatbot escalation to humans when the bot cannot answer effectively or detects user frustration or repeated rephrasing.
quote: Beyond explicit requests, chatbots should offer to escalate when they can no longer answer effectively or when the user shows signs of frustration or extra effort (e.g., repeatedly rephrasing the same question).

rule: Evaluate AI output rigorously before shipping; production speed must not outpace UX evaluation.
quote: Production has become cheaper than UX evaluation. It can now take less time to create an experience than to decide whether that experience is useful, usable, trustworthy, or coherent.

rule: Identify and fix AI-generated content that is awkward, generic, or obviously artificial before launch.
quote: Copy, graphics, and audio that are so obviously AI-generated that they become awkward distractions (and reputation killers)

rule: Remove AI features that add complexity without solving real user problems.
quote: Products overloaded with "smart" functionality that adds complexity but solves few real problems

rule: Never evaluate an AI system from a single output; test with multiple representative inputs and repeated runs.
quote: One good output demonstrates that a system can perform a task. It does not show how often or how reliably the system will do so.

rule: Do not substitute employee usage for user research; employees know too much to represent real users.
quote: They're insiders performing use, not real users encountering it fresh.

rule: Match the AI tool to your recurring task first; do not adopt based on demo performance alone.
quote: Before you spend money, change a workflow, or ask colleagues to adopt anything, define the task first: what would this tool help you do?

rule: Measure total time to complete work, not just AI generation time, to evaluate true velocity gains.
quote: Velocity: Measure Total Time, Not Generation Time

rule: Encode research findings and design standards as machine-readable context so any tool or person generates consistent output.
quote: Context enables you to avoid middle-of-the-road output.

rule: Curate raw research data and distill reasoning into AI-ready formats; traditional design documents do not serve AI models.
quote: A persona has a stock photo and a first name with the intention of helping a human to empathize and remember. However, a model does not need persuading, it needs the underlying reasoning.

rule: Lead with user value, not AI capability. Demonstrate how AI solves real problems before mentioning the technology.
quote: Companies should lead with the value that AI implementations offer rather than counting on AI to create value.

rule: Narrow the scope of AI features to increase user understanding and adoption.
quote: Narrowly scoped AI features are easier to understand and have better user adoption.

rule: Support users in writing effective prompts through hybrid interfaces combining text input with graphical controls.
quote: UIs that combine prompt-based inputs with a graphical user interface (GUI) can improve the usability of image-generation tools.

rule: Use contextually relevant, personalized, task-specific prompt suggestions matching user experience level.
quote: Prompt suggestions must be contextually relevant, personalized, and specific both to the task and to the user's level of experience.

rule: Use AI to enhance clarity and meet format constraints, but retain human editorial judgment for all substantive decisions.
quote: AI may contribute words and even some ideas to our articles, but humans remain responsible for editorial judgment.

rule: Have humans verify claims flagged by AI; AI identifies potential issues but never certifies correctness.
quote: AI never certifies that the claim is correct. When it flags an issue, it's the editor's or the author's job to go back to the source, double-check the claim, and correct the error if they find one.

rule: Build interactive AI prototypes with realistic data and multiple states early to surface edge cases before deployment.
quote: AI tools make it feasible to build fully interactive prototypes of complex interfaces so you can test them with users earlier in the design process.

rule: Test conversational AI with open-ended user input, not predetermined paths, to discover how agents handle unexpected requests.
quote: Study participants could input anything they'd like, rather than having to follow a predetermined path. As a result, the researchers could see how the agent handled unexpected requests.

rule: Focus design strategy on defining user needs and intent rather than pixel-pushing; curate meaningful context for AI.
quote: The core skills valuable today are moving more toward the pure UX work of defining user needs, specifying user intent, and overseeing the creation of excellent journeys — not the UI design of pushing pixels around in a design tool.

rule: Use AI only to organize and synthesize research you've already collected; never ask AI to generate user quotes or fill research gaps.
quote: AI can help you organize research you've already collected, but it can't create research evidence about the specific, messy experience of real users.

rule: Test checkout design changes systematically; research shows large sites gain up to 35% conversion uplift from checkout redesign.
quote: the average large-sized ecommerce site can gain as much as a 35% increase in conversion rate just by making design changes to their checkout process
finding: 35% conversion rate increase

rule: Evaluate designs against external standards to remove internal bias from objective assessment.
quote: An audit conducted against an external standard removes that bias.

rule: Benchmark mobile checkout against industry median and top quartile sites to calibrate competitiveness.
quote: how far below the median it sits, and what the top quartile of sites in your category looks like

rule: Audit designs before launch to reduce total cost of UX fixes, including development, testing, and redesign cycles.
quote: UX problems caught early — before a site redesign ships, a new checkout flow goes live, or mobile experience is revamped — are significantly cheaper to fix

rule: Interpret SUS scores by comparing them to percentile ranks from a normalized database of 10,000+ responses.
quote: Percentile ranks tell you how well your raw score compares to others in the database.
finding: Average SUS score is 68th percentile; scores above 68 are above average, below 68 are below average.

rule: When users rate a task below 5 on the SEQ, ask them to describe why they found it difficult.
quote: When a user provides a rating of less than 5 we ask them to briefly describe why they found the task difficult.

rule: Compare task difficulty ratings across competing products to isolate design friction from inherent task complexity.
quote: When possible we like to see how users do when attempting the same task on a comparable website to really gauge how difficult the task is relative to its inherent complexity.
finding: Users rate task difficulty 14% of the time inconsistently with actual task failure; differences average out across tasks.

rule: Use linear numeric scales to measure abstract concepts like satisfaction, ease, and likelihood to recommend.
quote: Linear numeric scales usually have at least the endpoints labeled.

rule: For long lists of 10+ items, use 'pick some' (fixed subset) instead of forced ranking to reduce cognitive load.
quote: This crude technique takes a fraction of the time as forced ranking and yields very similar results.

rule: Show result counts next to each filter option so users know if a selection narrows to zero.
quote: Show result counts next to each filter option — users need to know whether a selection will narrow the set to zero before they apply it

rule: Support multi-select within filter categories without requiring deselection.
quote: Support multi-select within filter categories — a user searching for blue or navy shoes should be able to select both without deselecting one to select the other

rule: Keep desktop filters visible in persistent panel; use sticky mobile drawer triggered by fixed button.
quote: On desktop, keep filters visible in a persistent panel. On mobile, use a sticky filter drawer triggered by a fixed 'Filter' button to keep controls accessible without consuming screen space.

rule: Provide thumbnails for every product item in the list without exception.
quote: Provide thumbnails for every item — no product in the list should be left without a visual representation

rule: Represent actual product accurately in thumbnails including quantities for multipacks.
quote: Represent the actual product accurately — thumbnails should clearly show what is being sold, including quantities (e.g. multipacks that may impact the user's perception of value

rule: Distinguish product attributes from title using spacing, line breaks, and distinct styling.
quote: Distinguish product attributes from the title — use spacing, line breaks, and distinct styling to separate attributes from the product name

rule: Present essential information like price and key attributes directly on list page.
quote: Present essential information like price and key product attributes directly on the list page

rule: Keep displayed attributes uniform across similar items to avoid user confusion.
quote: Keep the displayed attributes uniform across similar items to avoid user confusion

rule: Update main thumbnail when user selects color or variation via interactive swatches.
quote: Display options like color via interactive swatches and update the main thumbnail when a user selects a variation

rule: Choose research method to match the question, not the timeline or team familiarity.
quote: Teams often default to the method they know best, or the one that fits the timeline, rather than the one that actually fits the research question.

rule: Screen AI-generated images for diversity, representation, and authentic collaboration before use; inspect hands, text, reflections, and background details.
quote: Review representation: Who is shown, who is missing, and how are people portrayed? Assess authenticity: Do the people, setting, and interactions feel believable? Inspect for AI errors: Check text, hands, screens, glass reflections, and background details.

rule: Pair handmade visuals with human-sounding UX copy to reinforce authenticity and build trust.
quote: Voice is part of the aesthetic too. UX writing that sounds like a real person gives the same impression as handmade visuals. Pair handmade visuals with human-sounding copy.

rule: Credit the human artist by name in all promotions of handmade designs; authorship is a trust signal that distinguishes human work from AI.
quote: That emphasis on authorship matters now more than ever. With the right prompting, an AI tool could theoretically replicate this style. What it cannot replicate is the human story behind the work. That story is what gives the final result its value and makes it irreplaceable.

rule: Don't use warmth and handmade aesthetics to conceal product shortcomings; misaligned visual messaging undermines trust when product cannot deliver on promises.
quote: When the brand feels welcoming and secure, but the associated tool fails standards of security or accuracy, users will feel misled. Warmth that conceals the true attributes of a product undermines trust.

rule: Limit color palette to two main colors for visual balance and hierarchy; reserve extended color experimentation for designers with significant color expertise.
quote: In your own designs, limiting your color palette to just two colors will create balance and enforce visual hierarchy. Only if you have extensive color experience should you experiment with more complex color harmonies.

rule: Avoid neon colors; they distract users and reduce overall design effectiveness.
quote: Exercise caution with neon colors (such as highlighter yellow), as they may distract users and affect the overall effectiveness of the design.

rule: Apply more background blur to glassmorphic components when backgrounds are complex or intricate; less blur risks distracting users and harming text readability.
quote: More background blur is better, especially with intricate backgrounds (e.g., video, photography, animations).

rule: Use simple or single-color backgrounds behind glassmorphic components when you control the background; this reduces the need for extreme blur.
quote: If you have control of what appears behind a translucent component, opt for simple or single-color backgrounds.

rule: Check glassmorphic text contrast against multiple background colors using tools; text may have sufficient contrast only over certain areas of complex backgrounds.
quote: If you are designing a card component over a busy background, your text might only have enough contrast over certain areas and be challenging to read.

rule: Establish a dedicated team to maintain design systems continuously; without oversight, systems become outdated and lose utility.
quote: Design systems require continuous maintenance and oversight to ensure they do not become outdated, so a team is needed to manage it.

rule: Use subtle motion or transitions when the hamburger menu opens to reinforce the interaction and guide user expectations.
quote: Use subtle animation or transitions: If tapping the icon reveals a navigation panel, subtle motion cues can reinforce the interaction and guide user expectations.

rule: Scale the hamburger icon appropriately for screen size; a smartphone-sized icon becomes invisible on large desktop screens.
quote: Scale the hamburger icon appropriately: A hamburger icon sized for a smartphone can become nearly invisible on a large desktop screen.

rule: Provide additional navigation methods alongside the hamburger menu: inline links, related links lists, visible search, and footer links reduce interaction cost.
quote: Provide additional navigation methods: Support the hamburger with in-line links, lists of related links, a highly visible search function, and footer links.

rule: Add visual padding around the hamburger icon to increase visibility; crowding it near headers or other elements reduces discoverability.
quote: Add visual padding around the icon: Crowding the icon near headers or other UI elements reduces visibility.

rule: Display disabled buttons with reduced contrast and desaturated colors to signal they are not clickable.
quote: A light gray or otherwise desaturated color or a more muted version of its abled state to signal it isn't clickable or tappable

rule: Display focus state within 100–150ms using a stroke or outline, never color alone, to meet accessibility standards.
quote: focus state should appear pretty quickly (around 100-150ms) after the user uses the keyboard
finding: 100–150ms response time prevents users from tabbing repeatedly and missing buttons

rule: Show pressed state feedback within 100–150ms so users perceive the action as instantaneous.
quote: pressed state should appear within 100–150ms for the user to register that the pressing action is instantaneous
finding: 100–150ms feedback prevents users from pressing buttons multiple times

rule: Use stroke or outline for keyboard focus state, not color change alone, to accommodate users with vision impairments.
quote: stick to the stroke or outline to indicate focus, as opposed to relying on color change alone

rule: Add ARIA-disabled attribute to disabled buttons so screen readers announce their inactive state.
quote: Disabled button states should also have the ARIA-disabled: true attribute added to the code

rule: Restrict neobrutalist color palettes to 2–3 bold high-contrast colors to avoid overwhelming users.
quote: Restrict your palette to 2–3 bold, high-contrast colors (e.g., black, neon green, electric blue) to avoid overwhelming users

rule: Use generous padding of 24–32px margins in neobrutalist layouts to create breathing room and focus attention.
quote: offset dense geometric shapes and thick borders with generous padding (e.g., 24–32px margins) to create breathing room

rule: Pair bold, chunky headlines with clean, neutral body fonts like Roboto or Inter to maintain readability.
quote: Pair bold, unconventional headlines (e.g., a chunky sans-serif font) with clean, neutral body fonts like Roboto or Inter

rule: Use solid drop shadows offset by 4px instead of soft layered shadows to maintain neobrutalist raw aesthetics.
quote: a black drop shadow offset by 4px

rule: Conduct 5-second tests to capture users' initial visual impressions before they process details or read copy.
quote: Five seconds of viewing time is too short for reading copy or noticing details like specific fonts, but it is enough to formulate an impression of the visual style

rule: Avoid warning participants in 5-second tests that designs will be shown briefly, to capture authentic reactions.
quote: avoid warning participants that the design will be shown for only five seconds. This helps capture participants' authentic initial reactions

rule: Use first-click tests to verify users can locate information within seconds using task-specific goals.
quote: First-click tests tell you if users can accurately find what they need on your website

rule: Make design variations in preference testing significantly different enough for nondesigners to detect immediately.
quote: the differences must be significant enough to be immediately detectable to a nondesigner

rule: Counterbalance or randomize the order of design variations to prevent first-version bias in preference testing.
quote: counterbalance or randomize the order in which you present design variations to your participants

rule: Present behavioral tasks before aesthetic questions in combined usability and visual-design tests to avoid biasing task results.
quote: It's important to present behavioral tasks first and aesthetic assessments afterward

rule: Keep numerical rating questionnaires short; longer surveys increase likelihood of random or unmotivated responses.
quote: Short and easy questionnaires are ideal. The longer the questionnaire, the higher the chance of random answers

rule: Use closed word-choice testing to verify users perceive target brand attributes from design elements.
quote: Providing users with a limited set of words allows you to focus on whether participants pick up the target brand attributes

rule: Investigate time spent on tasks in detail; users spending long times may have completed tasks but experienced mentally taxing processes.
quote: Time spent is also worth investigating in detail, as it adds additional understanding of the mental effort involved in finding a resource.

rule: Mark multiple correct answers when testing polyhierarchy; review detailed destination data to see which correct answers users actually selected.
quote: you can mark multiple correct answers for the same task, and then review what proportion of your participants selected each of the correct answers

rule: Use polyhierarchy (cross-listing) only when data shows a substantial portion of users will look for an item in multiple parent categories.
quote: use polyhierarchy only if your data indicates that a substantial portion of your users will look for an item in multiple parent categories

rule: Compare task success rates within similar hierarchy depths, not across different depths; use own historical data as frame of reference.
quote: it would be more realistic to compare either: The success rate for the food-stamps task to that of another task which also targets content that is 6 levels down

rule: Use 50+ participants per tree for quantitative tree testing to achieve reasonably narrow confidence intervals and detect statistically significant differences.
quote: Typically, 50+ participants per tree are needed for a quantitative study to achieve reasonably narrow confidence intervals and find a statistically significant difference
finding: Sample size of 50+ per tree necessary for statistical significance in comparative studies.

rule: Conduct moderated pilot sessions before quantitative tree testing to verify task wording is understandable and catch nuances missed in quantitative data.
quote: We recommend beginning a quantitative tree test with a small qualitative study for two reasons: To pilot your study design and ensure that your tasks are understandable and do not bias participants. To obtain insights about why users chose the answers they did

rule: Use factual, neutral language in AI explanations; avoid first-person phrasing that anthropomorphizes the model's reasoning.
quote: Instead, use factual, neutral language (e.g., This answer is based on the following source: [link].)

rule: Avoid step-by-step explanations that imply certainty; provide sources and clarify limitations instead until true explainability improves.
quote: Given that step-by-step reasoning is often unreliable, designers should avoid using step-by-step explanations that imply certainty or transparency.

rule: Provide mock data in realistic format to guide AI-generated layouts; AI designs improve when working with actual content rather than placeholder abstractions.
quote: Providing sample content or data guides the AI to generate better designs.

rule: Assume most users will never see an info tip; design it for those confused or stuck, needing clear, immediate task guidance.
quote: assume that most users will never see the info tip. Those who do have extra motivation for seeking them out are confused, stuck, or need clarification or reassurance.

rule: Never hide form constraints, character limits, or legal disclaimers in info tips; display them at the primary level of the interface.
quote: any constraints, rules, or limitations for inputs should be displayed on the primary level.

rule: Keep info-tip content inline or adjacent to the element it supports; avoid modals, overlays, or new pages that disconnect users from their workflow.
quote: When possible, ensure that info tips are displayed inline or adjacent to the relevant element. Obscuring the current step or view of the interface makes it harder for users to connect the guidance with the task at hand.

rule: Use clear, descriptive link text starting with keywords; avoid vague labels like 'Get Started' or generic phrases that confuse user intent.
quote: Guidelines for writing link text

rule: Place different colors on visited and unvisited links to help users understand which content they have already explored.
quote: Change the Color of Visited Links

rule: Avoid cascading multilevel dropdown menus; use mega menus or landing pages instead.
quote: A simple dropdown menu works well for one-tier navigation but becomes frustrating with two tiers. It is highly inadvisable for more than two tiers, as it increases the risk of accidentally selecting the wrong subcategory or of closing the menu altogether.

rule: Present language options before any other audio content so callers can select their language immediately.
quote: If callers have the option to select their language, they should be given this choice immediately. Don't force callers to listen through lengthy messages in a language they don't understand
finding: US Customs required callers to wait 1 minute 22 seconds of English audio before Spanish/Chinese options appeared

rule: Warn callers and give them time to prepare before presenting detailed information like phone numbers, emails, or web addresses.
quote: Warn callers with phrases such as We would like to provide you with some other resources such as contact emails, phone numbers, and websites. You might want to grab a pen

rule: Speak technical information at half normal speed and offer options to repeat it or receive it via text.
quote: Present technical information twice as slowly as a normal speaking rate. Callers trying to remember or capture information such as a phone number will be very grateful.

rule: Use consistent keypad controls throughout the phone tree: same keys for undo, repeat, and other functions across all menus.
quote: The same keypad options should perform these two functions throughout the entire phone tree and the labels used for these functions should also be consistent throughout the design

rule: Always provide keypad selection as an alternative to voice-based natural language input in phone trees.
quote: Always provide an alternative navigation method — such as listening to menu options and making a selection. The difference between these methods is comparable to the value of providing meaningful navigation items in addition to the search bar on a website.

rule: Provide useful information outside operating hours: hours, FAQ pages, and emergency contact details.
quote: For organizations who have long periods without anyone answering the phones (such as overnight), there should still be useful information provided in a recording for callers

rule: Remove promotional statements and keep phone-tree messages concise; avoid lengthy advertisements or irrelevant details.
quote: Trapped callers do not want to listen to advertisements, promotions, or wordy messages that ramble on about things that are irrelevant and prevent them from accomplishing their current task

rule: Provide brief auditory confirmation when callers make a selection to show the system registered their choice.
quote: Provide brief feedback confirming callers' actions. When callers make a selection in a phone tree, they need clear feedback confirming that they made the choice they meant to or that their choice was registered by the system.

rule: Only share web addresses that directly relate to the caller's selected topic, not the homepage.
quote: A web address is helpful only if the corresponding page directly relates to a topic the caller has indicated is relevant. However, be cautious of long URLs that will be difficult to remember or write down.

rule: Choose user-friendly preferred terms for taxonomy concepts and link internal business jargon as nonpreferred synonyms.
quote: The best practice is to choose a user-friendly term as your preferred term and link internal business jargon or more technical language as nonpreferred synonyms.

rule: Place the required-field asterisk at the label's beginning in red to let users scan left edge quickly on longer forms.
quote: put it just before the field description is to help the eyes easily locate which fields are required by scanning just the left-most character of the label.

rule: Use calendar pickers only for dates within one year; for dates far in past or future, allow direct typing.
quote: Calendar pickers should be used for events close to the present time — within less than a year. However, they can be frustrating for users who choose dates far in advance because they require too much navigation

rule: Accept dates without leading zeros and in varied formats; parse user input as 9-3-17, 09/08/17, or 9/3/17 equivalently.
quote: Whatever format users chose for entering the date (dashes, spaces, slashes, dots between the month, day, and year components), their input should be recognized. Moreover, leftmost zeros should not affect the date.

rule: Disable and gray out illogical date pairs (return before departure, past dates) to prevent user error.
quote: Users should be prevented from entering a return date that takes place before the departure date or that is in the past. Make the choices clear by disabling and graying out options that are not available

rule: Ask for only essential information; eliminate nonessential, nonurgent, or irrelevant questions from forms.
quote: Forms should only ask for essential information — if a question isn't critical or relevant, eliminate it.

rule: Justify form questions to users, especially unexpected or sensitive ones, to build trust.
quote: A simple, clear explanation reassures users, builds trust, and helps them understand the rationale behind each question.

rule: Prefill form fields with existing data rather than asking users to re-enter information.
quote: If your organization has access to existing data — either from integrations or prior user submissions — use it to prefill form fields and allow users to verify or update the information as needed.

rule: Infer data from user input instead of asking separately; derive city and state from ZIP code, age from birthdate.
quote: Instead of asking users to provide information that can be easily inferred, use automation to streamline the process. For example, derive the city and state from a ZIP code or calculate age based on a birthdate.

rule: Use input masks to auto-format phone numbers, dates, and other structured data as users type.
quote: Input masks help users understand the correct format, prevent errors, and make it easier to doublecheck their input.

rule: Make checkbox labels and surrounding area clickable with a minimum 1 cm × 1 cm touch target.
quote: Include a perimeter around the checkbox and make the label clickable to allow for adequate touch-target size (at least 1 cm x 1 cm).

rule: Word checkbox labels positively to avoid double negatives that confuse users.
quote: Ensure that all your label statements are worded positively. Negatively worded statements force users to contemplate double negatives, leading to errors.

rule: Display checkbox lists vertically, never horizontally, to preserve scannability and label alignment.
quote: Display your list vertically. Vertical checkbox lists are easier to scan than horizontal ones.

rule: State minimum or maximum selection requirements explicitly and provide real-time visual feedback.
quote: Clearly state any requirements in the instructions and provide real-time visual feedback when the requirements have been satisfied or violated.

rule: Distribute surveys immediately after an event while memory is fresh to reduce recall bias.
quote: Distribute a survey to participants as soon as possible following the event related to your research. For example, if your survey asks why a user subscribed to a particular service, have the subscription act as a trigger for the survey, while their rationale for subscribing is as fresh as possible.

rule: Use ranges for sensitive data (age, income) rather than asking for exact numbers to reduce prestige bias.
quote: Providing age or income ranges will avoid requiring respondents to directly input their age or salary and will be less likely to result in a distortion.

rule: Use semantic-differential scales instead of Likert scales to reduce acquiescence bias in surveys.
quote: Use a semantic-differential scale rather than a Likert scale. A semantic-differential scale still asks participants to provide a rating but provides a continuum of response options specific to the nature of the question.

rule: Use progressive profiling to collect user data over time instead of demanding one long form upfront; customize questions to the buyer's intent.
quote: Rather than asking people to complete a long and tedious profile form, collect information about each prospect over time, by asking different questions that are customized to the situation and buyer's intent.

rule: Avoid sliders when users need to select a precise value; use them only for approximate ranges that satisfy the task.
quote: Sliders work best when the specific value does not matter to the user, but an approximate value is good enough. Thus, Kayak may get away with using sliders for duration and arrival and departure hours, as most users will be fine with a departure time that is, say, midday, and won't care to specify the exact moment of the departure.

rule: Place slider labels above or beside the control, never below, so they remain visible when the user's finger obscures the track.
quote: In order to remain visible during use, any labels describing the slider or its currently selected value must appear beside or above both thumbs involved: the thumb of the user, and the thumb of the slider (also known as the knob or elevator).

rule: Use helpful constraints to force users toward valid options; prevent backward-stepping errors like selecting a return date before departure.
quote: If users aren't limited in the dates they can choose, they may slip and accidentally select a set of dates for their flight that don't follow the rules. A helpful constraint here will force users to pick a date range that fits.

rule: Offer contextual autocomplete and search suggestions to prevent typos from breaking user goals, especially on touchscreens without haptic feedback.
quote: While you cannot prevent a user from making typos (which are slip-type errors), you can preempt typos from turning into problems by offering contextual suggestions while the user types.

rule: Offer sensible default values (e.g., reminders set to tomorrow) to prevent errors in repetitive tasks and teach users about reasonable choices.
quote: Especially when users have to perform repetitive actions, or in situations where they need to use precision, start by offering reasonable defaults that are likely to fit their real-world goals, and then allow them to refine their choices.

rule: Keep related content together on the same viewport to reduce cognitive load and back-and-forth scrolling.
quote: Keep critical, related content grouped together in the same viewport. Consider which information is most relevant to understanding the offering and choose designs that keep this content together to reduce back-and-forth scrolling.

rule: Avoid accordions on desktop; they fragment content and increase interaction cost compared to expanded layouts.
quote: Accordions can contribute to content fragmentation and significantly increase the interaction cost of finding crucial information, without the benefit they bring on mobile.

rule: Add scrolling cues at viewport edges to prevent illusion of completeness and signal more content below.
quote: If no scrolling cues exist to indicate that there is more content to discover, users are likely to miss this content.

rule: Support the Back button or gesture to dismiss bottom sheets to maintain expected navigation patterns.
quote: You can prevent this issue by supporting the use of Back for dismissing the bottom sheet, thus allowing the users to seamlessly return to the previous view.

rule: End alt text with a period to signal screen readers to pause, even for fragments.
quote: End alt text with a period, even if it isn't a full sentence. The period ensures that the screen reader pauses after reading the alt text.

rule: Avoid technical jargon and abbreviations in alt text unless users will certainly understand them.
quote: Avoid technical jargon and abbreviations unless users are certain to understand them.

rule: Never reuse alt text for the same image across different contexts; reanalyze the context each time.
quote: Never reuse alt text for the same image without reanalyzing the context in which the image is placed.

rule: Mention people's identity only if race, ethnicity, gender, religion, or culture is relevant to the image's purpose.
quote: Mention identity only if it's relevant. If the race, ethnicity, gender, religion, or cultural identifiers of the people pictured aren't part of the reason the image was included, don't mention them.

rule: For complex informative images, edit page copy to state the message as a list or table, making alt text unnecessary.
quote: Make complex informative images more accessible by altering the page copy surrounding the image. Editing the page copy to communicate the image's message often makes the visual itself redundant. In many cases, this could be as simple as including a list or table within the HTML of the page.

rule: Use long descriptions (structured text, lists, or tables) for complex images when page copy cannot be edited.
quote: Long descriptions house more detailed information than is reasonable to stuff into traditional alt text. They can include longer paragraphs of text, lists, or tables.

rule: Prioritize large-font captions and informative page copy over alt text for users with low vision.
quote: These users benefit more from meaningful, large-font image captions and informative page copy than from alt text.

rule: Allow guest checkout without mandatory account creation; offer registration only as an optional password field during purchase.
quote: Rather than forcing users to register before checking out, provide the option to register within the checkout process by presenting optional fields for the user to enter a password.
finding: Sites adding guest checkout immediately realize increased sales.

rule: Achieve WCAG 2 minimum contrast ratio (4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text) with desaturated colors on dark backgrounds, avoiding highly saturated hues.
quote: Highly saturated colors on dark backgrounds have poor visibility and do not comply with accessibility guidelines, such as the WCAG 2 requirement of a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

rule: Use one font color at varying opacity levels to maintain readability across different dark-mode background colors.
quote: When choosing the color of fonts in dark mode, use one color with different levels of opacity. This allows you to accommodate different background colors throughout the interface.

rule: Include visual design references and Figma links in prompts to AI tools; high-fidelity artifacts yield more accurate translations.
quote: An image is worth a thousand words proves remarkably accurate here. When AI tools can examine existing patterns, spatial relationships, hierarchy, and aesthetic treatments through the artifacts you provide, they can produce more consistent and accurate designs that match your vision.
finding: Prompts with attached Figma frames produced the most accurate translation of original designs compared to text-only prompts.

rule: Use specific, detailed text prompts with explicit design requirements; avoid vague language that forces AI to make assumptions.
quote: Longer prompts with clear, detailed design requirements consistently yield better results — particularly with AI tools that generate code-based prototypes, which can produce outputs that resemble the work of a human designer.
finding: Detailed text prompts (Prompt 2) generated outputs similar to human-designed versions; broad prompts (Prompt 1) varied widely across tools.

rule: Disambiguate design vocabulary in prompts; define whether terms like 'profile page' refer to social, personal, or enterprise contexts.
quote: When working with AI, designers need to disambiguate the language of their prompts as much as possible , so that they can precisely communicate the exact situation they need to design for.

rule: Use AI prototyping for ideation, early exploration, and proof-of-concept demos, not final production designs.
quote: AI's limited grasp of design nuances and inconsistent output make it best suited for ideation, concept exploration, and early-phase prototype testing, rather than later stages.

rule: Allow users to update their name everywhere in the product, including URLs and search indexes, without losing discoverability.
quote: Make names editable and reflect those changes everywhere in the product – even in URLs. Plan for gradual rollouts where both names work, at least temporarily, by default.

rule: Support easy account switching without forcing repeated logout and login cycles.
quote: Account switching should be trivial. Don't make people log out and back in every single time they want to change. In some cases, you can let people sign in once and then create multiple subaccounts or just associate multiple accounts with the same login information.

rule: Provide multiple recovery options for locked-out users that do not depend on the same device or method.
quote: Have multiple account-recovery options that don't all depend on the same device. Make your support-contact information findable and usable when someone isn't logged in.

rule: Design collaborative features to handle slow connections, real-time conflicts, and asynchronous editing with clear conflict resolution.
quote: Design for both asynchronous and real-time collaboration. Show clear conflict resolution. Make it obvious when someone's changes aren't saving.

rule: Cache data intelligently and provide offline-mode fallbacks for users with spotty internet connections.
quote: Offline-first design isn't just for developing countries. Cache intelligently, and, whenever possible, provide some sort of off-line mode. Show clear indicators of sync status.

rule: Build safety features, blocking, and reporting mechanisms from the ground up, not as reactive afterthoughts.
quote: Build safety features from the ground up, not only as a response to problems. Make blocking and reporting easy and effective.

rule: Use clear, descriptive section headings in forms to establish context and reduce cognitive load.
quote: Adding clear, descriptive headings to each section provides users with a helpful preview of the upcoming topic. These signposts reduce cognitive load by establishing context before users encounter specific fields.

rule: Use containers, divider lines, or colored backgrounds to reinforce visual groupings of form fields.
quote: If spacing doesn't provide enough clarity on how elements are related, reinforce groupings with containers, subtle divider lines, or colored backgrounds. This is the Gestalt principle of common region in action: visual boundaries help users quickly see which parts of the form belong together.

rule: Use single-column form layouts to provide a clear, predictable vertical path and improve accessibility.
quote: Research consistently shows that single-column layouts outperform multicolumn designs for form-completion rates. A single column provides a clear, vertical path that's easy to follow and scale across devices.

rule: Distinguish required fields from optional fields using both asterisks and explicit optional labels.
quote: If you decide to include optional questions, clearly distinguish them from required ones . In addition to using an asterisk to mark required fields, explicitly mark optional fields. This practice reassures users that they can skip nonessential questions and lightens their cognitive load.

rule: Display progress indicators on multipage forms to show completion status and motivate users to finish.
quote: Progress indicators give users a visual representation of how much they've filled and how much remains, helping them gauge the effort required to complete the form. This sense of progression also fosters a feeling of accomplishment, which in turn motivates users to continue until the end.

rule: Write form labels and instructions at the 6th to 8th-grade reading level; avoid jargon and internal terminology.
quote: We usually recommend writing at the 6th to 8th-grade reading level for general audiences — users shouldn't need to understand specialized vocabulary to fill your form. The most effective forms use language that mirrors how users naturally think and speak about the information being requested.

rule: Use positive, opt-in wording for checkboxes instead of negative statements that require mental reversal.
quote: Negative wording complicates how users interpret questions, as it forces them to mentally reverse statements. It increases cognitive effort and the risk of errors. This is especially relevant for standalone checkboxes — opt-in statements should use language that matches the intended outcome.

rule: Ask one question at a time in forms and surveys; avoid double-barreled questions.
quote: Double-barreled questions are questions that ask about two things at once ; they are a common survey pitfall. They introduce ambiguity as users might agree with one part but disagree with another.

rule: Use standard form element styles and behaviors; avoid novel interactions for checkboxes, radio buttons, and other controls.
quote: Users develop mental models about how form elements should look and behave based on their experiences across websites . Using consistent, familiar patterns allows users to apply existing knowledge and focus on the task at hand, rather than figuring out how the interface works.

rule: Match input field length to expected content length; short fields signal brief responses, long fields suggest detailed input.
quote: The size of an input field provides a visual cue about the expected length of the answer. A short field suggests a brief response , ideal for concise data like ZIP codes or age. A longer field implies that more detailed input is needed , such as an address, description, or comment.

rule: Place labels and help text outside input fields; never use placeholders as the sole instruction method.
quote: While placeholders — the text inside input fields that disappears when users tap into the field — may seem like a space-efficient way to provide guidance at first glance, they cause significant usability problems : They disappear when users start typing, forcing them to remember instructions using short-term memory .

rule: Use input constraints (e.g., character limits, amount caps) to prevent invalid data before users see error messages.
quote: In cases where clear rules define acceptable options, constraints become beneficial as they prevent users from making costly or time-consuming mistakes. Rather than letting users input invalid data and then showing an error message later, proactive constraints catch errors before they occur.

rule: Keep enriched search suggestions in a fixed layout; do not shift content types based on query.
quote: Maintain dedicated spaces for various content types (as opposed to shifting the location of specific types of enriched site-search suggestions based on queries).

rule: Label all enriched suggestion types explicitly to prevent users from interpreting them as promotional content.
quote: Clearly label the enriched suggestion types (e.g., top sellers, recommended products, recent searches) so that users do not have to guess what they're seeing or why it's being displayed.

rule: Preserve simple text autocomplete suggestions even when offering enriched search results.
quote: Do not eliminate simple text autosuggestions. Users heavily utilize these basic site-search suggestions even when enriched search suggestions are present.

rule: Limit graphical content in search suggestions to reduce loading delay and banner blindness.
quote: Limit the amount of graphical and dynamic content, which can cause slower loading times and contribute to banner blindness.

rule: Use plain language and common terms in content; accept imperfect search queries from users unfamiliar with domain terminology.
quote: focus on anticipating what language people might use to search for your products or content if they didn't know the correct term

rule: Deploy faceted filters to help users discover and learn specialized vocabulary in complex domains like car parts, skin care, and home improvement.
quote: Faceted systems can sometimes be helpful for formulating queries in unfamiliar domains

rule: When using branded terminology, include plain language alternatives alongside it for SEO and user education.
quote: If you do use branded terms, make sure you include the plain language alternative alongside it on the site

rule: In 20% of search queries, users look at only one result and rely on search engine ranking; trust in top placement drives this behavior.
quote: in 20% of the 377 search instances, people looked at only one result on the SERP
finding: 20% of queries involve fixation on only one SERP element; statistically significant increase from 17% in 2006 (p < 0.001)

rule: Position critical answers in distinctive SERP features (featured snippets, tables, panels) to attract immediate attention and satisfy search intent.
quote: SERP features like the featured snippet always look distinct compared to organic search results and guide the eyes

rule: Tailor content to address users' precise questions to increase likelihood of being featured in prominent SERP positions where users focus their gaze.
quote: They should understand their users' needs and questions and tailor their content so that it addresses those questions precisely

rule: Target subsecond load times as the ideal; prioritize each incremental speed gain over settling for average.
quote: Subsecond load times would be ideal; realistically, this target is incredibly difficult to achieve while also delivering rich and engaging content.

rule: Delay hover-triggered content 0.3–0.5 seconds to confirm intent before exposing large disruptive overlays.
quote: after the mouse cursor paused movement and remained in the target area for around 0.3–0.5 seconds, at which time the hidden content can safely be animated onto the page.

rule: Wait 0.5 seconds after cursor leaves a hover target before collapsing exposed content to tolerate minor mouse drift.
quote: Only if the user has clicked or tapped outside of the target area, or the mouse cursor has left the target area and exposed content for longer than 0.5 seconds, can the intent to collapse the exposed content be determined.

rule: Design for low-end users lagging 2–3 years behind high-end bandwidth; avoid bloated designs even as speeds increase.
quote: The vast masses of users are low-end and will lag 2–3 years behind the high-end users.

rule: Optimize for download speed as the dominant design criterion until bandwidth reaches 1.5 Mbps; minimize design complexity.
quote: For the next 5 years, the web will be dominated by users with such slow connections that any reasonable web page will take much longer to download than the response time limits indicated by human factors research. Thus, the dominant design criterion will be download speed in all web projects until about the Year 2003. Minimalist design rules.

rule: Use realistic mock data in prototypes because users scrutinize unfamiliar tables and charts for outliers and inconsistencies.
quote: Research in data sensemaking by Laura Koesten and colleagues found that when participants were given unfamiliar data, they spent more time looking for outliers and inconsistencies than when they worked with familiar data.

rule: Contextualize mock table data to audience size, industry, geography, and market to avoid unrealistic values.
quote: Your table will be less helpful if your AI is modeling data for a large enterprise when your app targets mall businesses. For example, business size, industry or market, geography, or time periods can all influence the table's data.

rule: Account for full dataset size when generating subset rows so values remain plausible relative to the whole.
quote: The dataset may be much larger. Describe the size of the larger dataset, if known, so the AI can account for these additional records when calculating values.

rule: Request SVG format for AI-generated charts to preserve editability of elements in design tools.
quote: Generating charts in SVG format makes them easy to import and edit in design tools like Figma.

rule: Place task-relevant content in primary areas; users ignore sidebars with irrelevant promotions or ads.
quote: the right rail had a fair-to-high concentration of irrelevant content, users were likely to quickly abandon it even if they happened to glance at it
finding: In Baidu studies, pinball patterns appeared in 1 of 60+ searches; Google showed many pinball patterns due to relevant knowledge panels in sidebars.

rule: Promote internal products only when directly relevant to the user's current search query.
quote: it's okay to promote your content on the SERP, as long as it is relevant to the user's task
finding: When Baidu promoted relevant content (Summer Palace trip planning), users felt informed. When promotions were irrelevant, users developed banner blindness within a year.

rule: Include images or visual elements in search results to act as quick signposts that verify result relevance.
quote: SERP features — particularly the ones with images and video thumbnails — can take on the role that logos play on a webpage: they act as signposts that enable users to quickly verify that the results are indeed for the entity they are interested in
finding: Users immediately corrected off-topic searches (e.g., snake photos for 'copperhead' instead of Civil War faction) when visual signposts clarified intent.

rule: Design featured snippets to mimic natural language query expansion; show related questions without requiring users to reformulate.
quote: most users are terrible at generating alternate search strategies. But through SERP features, Google can present several expanded interpretations of the query in natural language and allow the user to explore those alternatives without leaving the page
finding: Users clicked related questions in 'People Also Ask' because interaction cost was low (no page load) and benefit was high (answers already visible).

rule: Use 'People Also Ask' accordions to redirect user tasks; loaded questions should relate to the clicked question.
quote: When one accordion is opened, Google loads more questions into the feature, usually related to the question that was clicked
finding: One user searching for Botox cost saw 'Is Botox safe?' question, which changed her entire task goal to 'noninvasive approaches' after reading safety concerns.

rule: Present simple facts (addresses, phone numbers, definitions, dates) in consistent, scannable formats on results pages.
quote: When people are searching for simple facts (statistics, dates, deadlines, addresses, phone numbers, etc.), they don't need to click on a search result anymore: Google can scan a website for that information and present it to them in a consistent, easily scannable format
finding: Users read featured snippets for quick facts and ended tasks without clicking through, saving time and effort.

rule: Signal changes far from the user's current focus with stronger visual cues than simple replacement.
quote: Changes outside the user's field of vision might be overlooked and require stronger signaling than simply replacing the old information with something new

rule: Allow extra time for users with language barriers or disabilities to process rapidly changing screens.
quote: This is particularly problematic for slower users, such as international customers who don't read your language well or old or disabled users

rule: Achieve 0.1-second response to direct user actions to create the illusion of direct manipulation.
quote: 0.1 seconds gives the feeling of instantaneous response — that is, the outcome feels like it was caused by the user, not the computer

rule: Respond within 10 seconds maximum or users will abandon the task and lose focus.
quote: After 10 seconds, they start thinking about other things, making it harder to get their brains back on track once the computer finally does respond

rule: Reduce response time by even 0.1 seconds to lift conversion rates measurably.
quote: When sites shave as little as 0.1 seconds off response time, the outcome is a juicy lift in conversion rates
finding: 0.1-second improvement yields measurable conversion lift

rule: Replace heavy server processing and complex widgets with simpler, faster alternatives.
quote: today's big response-time sinners are typically overly complex data processing on the server or overly fancy widgets on the page

rule: Deliver visual impressions in under 50 milliseconds; users form rough design judgments in this window.
quote: people can make rough decisions about a web page's visual appeal after being exposed to it for as little as 50 ms
finding: 50 ms (0.05 seconds) is sufficient for users to distinguish attractive from unattractive designs

rule: Limit videos to 1–2 minutes because passive viewing bores web users in active mode.
quote: most internet videos should last no more than 1–2 minutes because people don't like passively watching something for much longer than that while they're in the active frame of mind induced by web surfing

rule: Support revisitation by tracking user progress across multiple visits spanning days or weeks.
quote: sites must support revisitation behaviors, for example by keeping track of what users have done in previous visits

rule: Limit compare tools to show no more than 5 products side by side; do not require users to compare more alternatives than working memory can handle.
quote: Compare tools that allow users to select a few products and directly compare them are also helpful. Remember that there is no need to support more than about 5 products in each of these tools

rule: Show both positive and negative attributes for each alternative so users can determine whether benefits outweigh drawbacks.
quote: Even when evaluating a single item, people must see both the pros and cons to determine whether there are enough benefits to outweigh any negative aspects

rule: Implement multiword search that filters results to items matching every word in the query, not items matching any word separately.
quote: a user searching a site for 'wooden box' would expect to receive a list including only boxes that were made of wood — not all items on the site that are wooden plus all items that are boxes
finding: In-site searches contain an average of 2.3 words per query, including color, size, and brand

rule: Use consistent SERP layouts across queries so users don't reassess the page structure with each result.
quote: if you're designing SERPs for your in-site search, it's a better bet to use a consistent layout that doesn't change radically from query to query

rule: For research tasks, place critical information below the fold; 20% of selections occur there vs. 5% for fact-finding.
quote: 20% of selections in research tasks were below the fold. Both scenarios confirm the disproportionately high importance of information above the fold on web pages
finding: 20% of research-task selections below fold vs. 5% for fact-finding tasks

rule: Embed site-specific search boxes in top results; display the search query syntax to teach advanced search operators.
quote: Displaying the command in the search box is a good method to raise awareness of advanced search commands, which are virtually never used by the general web audience

rule: Limit SERP decision time; users spend 5.7 seconds on average before selecting the first result.
quote: users spent an average of 5.7 seconds considering results before they made their first selection (with a 95% confidence interval from 4.9 to 6.5 seconds)
finding: Average 5.7 seconds (95% CI: 4.9–6.5) before first selection

rule: Account for passive browsing; 14% of critical incidents in 2019 involve accidental discovery vs. 4% in 1997.
quote: a larger proportion of the reported instances in the new study involved passive information acquisition (14% versus only 4% in 1997 — the difference was statistically significant, p < 0.05)
finding: Passive acquisition grew from 4% (1997) to 14% (2019); statistically significant (p < 0.05)

rule: Support smartphone use as primary; 42% of critical incidents occur on smartphones vs. desktop.
quote: we found that most of the critical incidents (42%) occurred when people were using their smartphones — critical smartphone use was higher than critical desktop use
finding: 42% of critical incidents on smartphones vs. desktop (p < 0.05)

rule: Enable social inquiry in purchase flows; 67% of Product Info & Purchase social interactions are inquiries to companies.
quote: for Product Info & Purchase decisions, though only 20% of instances had accompanying social-interaction behavior, 67% of their social interaction was Inquire
finding: 67% of social interactions in purchase decisions are inquiries to companies

rule: Show immediate visual feedback for all actions; users assume unacknowledged clicks failed and try again.
quote: Without any visual change from the system, most users will assume the action was not registered and they will try again

rule: Use looped spinners only for 2–10 second delays; avoid for sub-1-second or longer waits.
quote: This indicator should be reserved for actions that take between 2-10 seconds. For anything that takes less than 1 second to load, it is distracting to use a looped animation

rule: Use percent-done bars for waits ≥10 seconds; users grow impatient with indefinite spinners.
quote: we don't recommend looped animation for actions that take longer than 10 seconds, because users quickly grow impatient if they feel like they aren't making progress

rule: Animate progress bars slower at start, faster toward end to avoid disappointment and sustain satisfaction.
quote: Start the progressive animation slower and allow it to move faster as it approaches the end. This way you don't risk establishing a faster expectation than the system can maintain. Exceeding customer expectations always creates more satisfaction than disappointing customers

rule: Progress indicators triple wait tolerance; users wait 3× longer with feedback than without.
quote: the people who saw the moving feedback bar experienced higher satisfaction and were willing to wait on average 3 times longer than those who did not see any progress indicators
finding: Users willing to wait 3× longer with animated progress bar vs. no indicator

rule: Allow users to cancel long processes; don't hijack system control during waits ≥10 seconds.
quote: For actions that take a little while, give users the option to stop the process, in case they decide they cannot wait. Otherwise, your design may be hijacking control of the system

rule: Use fixed column headers so users never lose column identity while scanning comparison tables downward.
quote: use fixed table headers, so that column titles are always visible. This prevents users from having to look all the way back at the top of page, potentially losing their place in the table.

rule: Let users hide irrelevant products in multi-column tables to preserve the lawn-mower scanning pattern.
quote: Allow them to hide products or services that they are not interested in, if your table has more than 2 columns.

rule: Group Yes/No and checkmark rows together to avoid disrupting the lawn-mower pattern.
quote: Group Yes/No Features Together

rule: Move empty or placeholder rows to the end of the table, never in the middle of active scanning content.
quote: When users scan the table in a lawn mower pattern, it's likely that they will accidentally scan the placeholder content, which provides no information.

rule: Use clear noticeable headings to break content into scannable sections.
quote: Using clear, noticeable headings and subheadings to break up content and label sections so that people can scan to find only what they're most interested in

rule: Place important information up front in content structure, subheadings, and links.
quote: Placing information up front (in other words, "front-loading") in the structure of our content, as well as in subheadings and links, to allow people to understand the message quickly while scanning

rule: Use bulleted lists and bold text to focus the eye on the most important information.
quote: Employing formatting techniques like bulleted lists and bold text to allow the eye to focus on the most important information

rule: Keep online content concise and use plain language for clarity.
quote: Using plain language to keep content concise and clear

rule: Avoid pull quotes and inline ads mid-article; they disrupt scanning and cause attention dropout.
quote: they tended to disrupt reading. Several participants in our study began reading articles nearly linearly and completely until they hit a pull quote or inline ad. After reaching one of those elements, the participants abandoned their reading and fell into light scanning.

rule: Bold, color, or link important words to trigger spotted-pattern scanning over inefficient F-pattern.
quote: They visually stand out in the text because they are styled differently (e.g., links, differently colored words, bolded words, bulleted lists).

rule: Use meaningful headings and subheadings; the layer-cake pattern with headings is far more effective than F-pattern scanning.
quote: Aside from reading almost every word, the layer-cake pattern is by far the most effective way in which users can scan pages.

rule: Chunk content with subheadings and call-out points even for motivated readers seeking deep comprehension.
quote: even for the commitment pattern, text comprehension is improved when the content is chunked and calls out its main points in subheadings.

rule: Avoid placing legitimate content in traditional ad locations (top banner, right rail) where users habitually ignore ads.
quote: Because desktop ads typically appear at the top of the page or in the right rail, web users sometimes ignore the content placed there.

rule: Do not style content with colors, backgrounds, or formatting that distinguish it from surrounding elements, as users mistake visually distinct items for ads.
quote: Anything that stands out from immediate surrounding context is likely to be considered an ad, although its presentation may be consistent with other elements on the page that are not visible at the time.

rule: On mobile, avoid inline ads within scrollable content; they occupy too much screen proportion for users to avert their gaze and interrupt reading flow.
quote: A mobile inline ad is so large in proportion to the screen size that users cannot avert their eyes from it as they swipe down.

rule: Use consistent visual treatment (typeface, color, size, or weight) to signal hierarchy between body text and subheadings without making subheadings resemble promotions.
quote: Marking subheadings so they visually stand out relative to the rest of the text in a consistent, predictable manner

rule: Use visual styling like headers and bold text to signal importance and help users locate new content sections.
quote: Users rely on elements like headers and bolded text to identify when information is important, and to locate new segments of content.

rule: Include visual signifiers such as cut-off text to show users that scrollable content exists below the fold.
quote: Include signifiers (such as cut-off text) to tell people that there is content below the fold.

rule: Place the most important points in the first two paragraphs to align with users' natural scanning focus.
quote: Include the most important points in the first two paragraphs on the page.
finding: First lines receive more gazes than subsequent lines; first few words on left receive more fixations than words to the right

rule: Follow established web-design conventions for element placement; only deviate if usability research proves dramatic improvement.
quote: If you're considering a design that deviates from web conventions, test it thoroughly and use it only if all your usability research indicates that it is dramatically better than the norm.
finding: Logo in upper-left found in fraction of a second; centered logo took at least 1-2 seconds and triggered exhaustive review scanning

rule: Adapt tone to user emotion: empathetic in errors, encouraging in onboarding, neutral on reference content.
quote: Your tone will shift depending on context: more empathetic in an error message, more encouraging in onboarding, more neutral on a policy page.

rule: Use jargon only when user research confirms your audience understands and prefers technical terms.
quote: Use jargon only when your audience expects and uses it. Before including a word that could be unclear to some users, make sure you have evidence from user research, survey data, or site-search logs that your audience understands and prefers a technical term.

rule: Use descriptive link text that communicates destination, not generic labels like "Learn More" or "Click Here".
quote: Learn More is a lazy link or button label. It tells users nothing about what they'll learn or where they'll go after clicking. It's also a significant accessibility failure: screen readers will announce Learn More, Learn More, Learn More, across a page with no way to distinguish among them.

rule: Use icon-triggered search cautiously; reduced prominence causes users to miss the feature entirely.
quote: However, use this with caution, as its reduced prominence can mean some users miss it altogether.

rule: Display key specifications first, before less critical attributes, to prioritize user decision-making information.
quote: display key details first, and use row styling so users can easily match labels to values

rule: Use alternating row backgrounds or subtle borders in spec tables to help users track labels across to their values.
quote: Use alternating backgrounds or subtle borders within the table to connect labels directly to their values and make it easier for users to scan

rule: Measure and track spec sheet UX performance; 64% of ecommerce sites have poor or mediocre spec sheet design.
quote: almost two-thirds (64%) of ecommerce sites' spec sheets are poor or mediocre
finding: 64% of ecommerce sites' spec sheet UX performance is poor or mediocre

rule: Ensure identical attribute labels, ordering, and units across all products of the same type; 30% of sites fail this.
quote: 30% of sites have severe issues with specs across products of the same type
finding: 30% of sites have severe issues with specs across products of the same type

rule: Reserve badges for information that genuinely influences purchase decisions; omit universal, obvious, or low-value attributes.
quote: A badge should only appear when the information it communicates would genuinely influence a user's decision to click through or purchase

rule: Write badge copy as 1–2 words maximum using plain language; avoid internal campaign names or vague promotional wording.
quote: Badge labels need to be short, concrete, and self-explanatory, because they're consumed during rapid scanning. Avoid brand-specific phrases, internal campaign names, or vague promotional wording

rule: Frame usability issues using loss aversion: present data showing what users will lose, not what they gain.
quote: stakeholders were much more likely to act on suggested changes when the data was presented with a negative frame. It aligns directly with game theory and loss aversion: the pain of a potential loss is psychologically far more powerful than the pleasure of a gain.
finding: Stakeholders act more readily on negative framing (e.g., '20% of users struggled') than positive ('80% had no issues').

rule: Rate usability issue severity by user impact, not by fix difficulty or your personal preference.
quote: Rate based on likely user impact, not your personal reaction to the issue, and not how easy the fix would be.

rule: Conduct mobile heuristic evaluations in a separate dedicated session, not as a spot-check at the end of desktop review.
quote: Conduct a separate mobile evaluation pass for each flow and treat it as a distinct evaluation, not a quick spot-check at the end of a desktop session.
finding: 75% of mobile ecommerce sites are only "Mediocre" according to large-scale usability testing; mobile-specific violations are underrepresented when evaluated with desktop.

rule: Test error states and edge cases deliberately during heuristic evaluation, not only the successful path.
quote: Many heuristic violations occur in error states, edge cases, and recovery paths.

rule: Use AI to code open-ended survey responses; it now matches human coder agreement and exceeds prior model consistency.
quote: human-to-ChatGPT-5.6 agreement (0.749) was statistically indistinguishable from human-to-human agreement (0.704, p = .475)
finding: ChatGPT-5.6 kappa agreement with humans: 0.749 (substantial); human-to-human: 0.704; ChatGPT-5.6 self-consistency: 0.950 (almost perfect)

rule: Prompt explicitly for edge-case handling; ambiguous responses caused variance in AI coding (e.g. 'Na', 'Not sure') across runs.
quote: Subtle shifts in classification like this could lead to lower agreement. Fortunately, this type of model variance can likely be mitigated with a more explicit prompt instruction regarding edge-case handling.

rule: AI moderators will dominate conversation; in in-depth interviews, plan for AI to speak 80% more than human moderators despite identical scripts.
quote: Human moderators spoke on average 55 WPM compared to AI moderators' 99 WPM. That is, on average, AI moderators were speaking 80% more than human moderators.
finding: AI moderator WPM: 99 vs human: 55 (80% more); participant-to-moderator word ratio: AI 0.5 vs human 1.8

rule: Use 11-point NPS scales consistently; switching to 10 or 5-point scales introduces 4% average scoring error.
quote: The average absolute difference when changing scales is around 4 percentage points
finding: Mean absolute difference of 4 percentage points between 11-point and 10-point scales; same for 5-point scales

rule: Avoid 10-point NPS scales; they reduce detractors by 8% without reducing promoters, inflating loyalty scores.
quote: The 10-point variation reduced the proportion of detractors (around 8%) without a corresponding reducing in promoters (they slightly increased)
finding: 8% reduction in detractors; 2.2% increase in promoters with 10-point scale

rule: Budget $7–$10 per general consumer participant for unmoderated online panel recruitment; $40–$100 for specialized profiles.
quote: the lowest cost per participant will range from between $7 and $10 (general consumer profile) and go up substantially to $40 to $100 (specialized profiles
finding: $7–$10 general, $40–$100 specialized profiles; minimum project $1,500

rule: Budget $100–$300 per qualified participant for external moderated recruitment, plus $12K–$15K for 20 participants with qualifications.
quote: They tend to charge between $100 and $300 to find each qualified participant and charge a project management fee
finding: $100–$300 per qualified participant; $12K–$15K total for 20 moderated participants with qualifications

rule: Budget $25 to $75 per participant for Western European and Asian recruitment; at least twice U.S. costs.
quote: Western European and Asian markets are usually at least twice the cost per complete as U.S. markets (they can be as high as $25 to $75 per participant)
finding: 2× U.S. costs; $25–$75 per participant in Western Europe and Asia

rule: Measure AI productivity gains; a 2026 Anthropic survey found 86% of users reported work speed improvements.
