quote: Results from an Anthropic survey indicated 86% of respondents reported improvements in the speed of their work.
finding: 86% of AI users reported improvements in work speed

rule: Use rating scale standard deviations of 20–28% of maximum range instead of 50% for binary data to reduce sample size needs substantially.
quote: All else being equal, sample size requirements based on these estimates (from 20–28%) will be substantially lower than estimates based on the standard deviation of binomial metrics (which is 50% of the range of the scale when p = .5).
finding: Rating scales cut sample size 2–4× compared to binary metrics for same precision

rule: For ±2-point margin of error on a 0–100 rating scale at 95% confidence, use n=603 with typical standard deviation instead of n=2,398 for binary metrics.
quote: At a margin of error of ±2 points, you'd need 2,398 participants using a binary metric. You would need just a quarter of that (603) using the typical rating scale's standard deviation of 25% of the maximum range.
finding: Rating scales reduce sample size to 25% of binary metric requirement for ±2% margin of error

rule: For multi-item questionnaires, use standard deviation of 20% of scale range to estimate sample size when no historical data exists.
quote: If your primary analyses will be multi-item questionnaires, it's reasonable to use the 's = 20' column.

rule: Use AI moderators for structured, high-volume data collection; reserve human moderators for discovery and studies requiring judgment about when and how to probe.
quote: For structured, high-volume, consistency-driven data collection, an AI moderator seems like a reasonable tool today. For discovery, emotional nuance, and studies where the whole point is to find what you didn't know to ask about, the human moderator isn't going anywhere yet.

rule: Use two or three colors in information hierarchy instead of many, as excessive colors diminish visual hierarchy and reduce effectiveness.
quote: Color helps highlight specific information, but do so sparingly, as too many colors make it harder to discern the hierarchy, diminishing their purpose.

rule: In remote sessions, look at the camera lens rather than the participant's video feed to register as eye contact on their screen.
quote: On camera, look at the lens, not the face. In a remote session, eye contact with the participant's video feed doesn't register as eye contact on their end. Looking at the camera does.

rule: Ask participants to subcategorize or combine cards when keyword matching occurs to encourage deeper conceptual thinking.
quote: If your participants engage in keyword matching, try asking them to subcategorize cards or combine cards into a larger group.

rule: Allow participants to make iterative changes to groupings after initial sorting and follow-up questions about placement difficulty.
quote: Allow participants to make iterative changes to their groupings. After their initial sort, ask users follow-up questions such as: Were any items especially easy or difficult to place?

rule: Recruit at least 15 participants for qualitative card-sorting studies to understand reasoning behind groupings.
quote: Researchers need to recruit at least 15 participants for this approach.
finding: minimum 15 participants for qualitative card sorts

rule: Recruit 30–50 participants for quantitative card-sorting studies to ensure results are generalizable to broader populations.
quote: For quantitative studies, we recommend at least 30–50 participants to ensure that results are generalizable to a broader population.
finding: 30–50 participants for quantitative card sorts to ensure generalizability

rule: Ask follow-up questions after card sorting to understand rationale, such as difficulty of placement and cards belonging to multiple groups.
quote: Were any items especially easy or difficult to place? Did any items seem to belong in two or more groups?

rule: Run a few moderated card-sorting sessions alongside quantitative unmoderated studies to understand participant reasoning and label clarity issues.
quote: Even if you run a quantitative unmoderated card sort, it's important to run a few moderated sessions to understand what participants are thinking as they group items.

rule: Use numerals instead of spelled-out words when displaying numbers in digital copy.
quote: Show Numbers as Numerals When Writing for Online Readers

rule: Place the most important words in the first two words of links and headlines to support scanning.
quote: First 2 Words: A Signal for the Scanning Eye

rule: Use plain language that users understand on first reading, regardless of their expertise.
quote: Plain language can be understood the first time your audience reads or hears it.

rule: Track product-team time savings and late-stage content requests to measure content-standards impact.
quote: start tracking product and content teams' time savings as concrete evidence of improvement

rule: Embed content standards within the design system rather than isolated PDFs to accelerate design decisions.
quote: embedding these standards within component design systems can significantly improve collaboration between UI and content designers

rule: Select two to three items per construct to measure AI UX attitudes, targeting scale reliability of at least 0.70.
quote: Our typical target for measuring a construct at this stage of questionnaire development is to select two to three items per construct with the goal of achieving scale reliability (measured with coefficient alpha) of at least 0.70 for each construct.
finding: All streamlined scales exceeded 0.80 coefficient alpha (range 0.81–0.87), exceeding the 0.70 research benchmark.

rule: Measure AI UX across six core constructs: Productivity, Trust, Dependency, Anxiety, Personification, and Early Adoption.
quote: We identified 34 candidate items across six constructs (AI Productivity, AI Trust, AI Dependency, AI Anxiety, AI Personification, and Early Adoption)

rule: Test content with users early to understand their questions and knowledge gaps before creating new content.
quote: Review existing data and test content with users to understand the questions they have and the knowledge gaps that new content or improvements to existing content can fill.

rule: Review and govern content at least every 3 months to decide whether to improve, replace, or remove low-performing content.
quote: Start with at least a 3-month interval for reviewing content and supporting collateral.

rule: Design content frames early in ideation before commencing visual design, not late when content becomes a problem.
quote: Use content frames for early ideation and exploration before design activities begin. Make sure that content is brought in at the very beginning; not when someone realizes the content is a mess.

rule: Design for long-term user needs like habit-building and self-confidence, not just short-term tasks, to enable lasting delight.
quote: if the defined function of that application was to help people build healthy habits and self-confidence, then it could deliver so much more value in addition to the exercises

rule: Structure context so it is discoverable and usable for models, not just stored; apply information architecture principles to context itself.
quote: A structure like this does more than help the user find files: it also controls which context the agent loads.

rule: Keep context files short, under a few hundred lines; anything longer probably contains material that doesn't need to load every time.
quote: Most participants kept files under a few hundred lines. Anything much longer probably contains material that doesn't need to load every time Claude references the file.

rule: Identify and remove barriers to desired user actions before optimizing benefits; test one intervention at a time.
quote: Here you choose one barrier to remove or one benefit to strengthen, then design a solution around it. You can't solve everything at once, so prioritize the barrier or benefit most likely to influence the target behavior.

rule: Use diverse imagery and identity cues matching target audience; avoid showing only idealized fitness outcomes.
quote: Show diverse members with different body types, ages, and fitness levels; not just highly fit 'after' images.

rule: Companies applying behavioral economics effectively can outperform peers by 85% in sales growth and more than 25% in gross margin.
quote: In fact, Gallup reports that companies that apply behavioral economics effectively can outperform peers by 85% in sales growth and more than 25% in gross margin.
finding: 85% sales growth improvement, 25% gross margin improvement

rule: Use breadcrumbs and section headers to help task-switching users quickly recognize their location without full reorientation.
quote: With serial task switching, users often bounce back to an app after only a short interruption. They're not fully recontextualizing, they just need quick indicators to recognize where they are and what they're looking at.

rule: Keep background tasks visible but unobtrusive using collapsible popups to support parallel work without blocking primary interface.
quote: While designing for parallel tasks, keep tasks that are in progress visible but unobtrusive. Use collapsible popups that remain visible as the user navigates, and avoid blocking important interface elements.

rule: Provide undo functionality for accelerator-triggered actions to recover from accidental activation.
quote: Provide a safety net for users to undo actions performed via accelerators on the off chance that they triggered them accidentally.

rule: Maintain accelerator consistency across platforms so common shortcuts work identically on web, mobile, and desktop.
quote: make sure that common shortcuts and gestures are consistent across platforms. For example, a double-tap-to-react feature should work the same in a mobile app as it does on a responsive website

rule: Never override platform-standard shortcuts like copy, paste, select-all, and print to prevent errors.
quote: Do not override commonly known shortcuts, such as those for copy, paste, select all, and print, to prevent errors and accelerate learning

rule: Use plural pronouns and collaborative framing during design reviews to build shared ownership across the team.
quote: Adjust your language to use more first-person-plural pronouns like 'we' and 'our,' and be careful with 'my.'

rule: Use radio buttons instead of dropdowns for 6 or fewer options to expose all choices immediately with single-click selection.
quote: The U.S. Web Design System (USWDS) recommends radio buttons for fewer than 7 items. Google Material Design (M3) sets the threshold at 6 items
finding: USWDS threshold: 7 items; M3 threshold: 6 items; IBM Carbon: 3 items

rule: Use a combobox with text filtering for dropdown lists exceeding roughly 15 options to reduce scanning burden and fine-motor control demands.
quote: When a list exceeds roughly 15 options, such as a country list (200+ options), the interaction cost of visually scanning it and the fine-motor control required to scroll through it can be overwhelming. In these scenarios, a combobox — a text field paired with a filterable dropdown list — helps alleviate the burden
finding: Threshold: ~15 options before combobox becomes necessary

rule: Replace dropdowns with button variants or swatches for visual product comparisons to enable simultaneous visibility and immediate feedback on stock status.
quote: laying out options as buttons surfaces all choices at once, allowing users to scan, compare, and select in one step. It also makes out-of-stock variants immediately apparent (e.g., through a grayed-out size), saving users from the frustration of going through a long list to select an option only to learn it's unavailable

rule: Show timestamps or last-update indicators on dynamic crisis information to build trust and confirm data freshness when user decisions depend on accuracy.
quote: Lastly, and importantly, it indicates when the map was last updated, to promote trust and reassure customers that they are not looking at stale data

rule: Keep icons visually distinct from each other and from competitors' icons to aid recognition and recall.
quote: Images that differ from the imagery around them are more likely to be noticed, processed, and therefore, remembered. In contrast, images that are too similar may be associated with similar words and may be harder to distinguish from each other and recall.

rule: Observe expert users working in their actual environment, not in labs, to discover contextual factors that shape system use.
quote: Real-world conditions — such as environmental constraints, interruptions, shared equipment, or cross-team coordination — shape how systems are actually used.

rule: Use scenario-based interviews and discussion with domain experts to assess reasoning, not just task completion accuracy.
quote: ask them to walk through how they would interpret and act on the data presented. Rather than focusing on whether users complete a task correctly, the team observes how the users reason through the decision

rule: Prototype at low fidelity—sketches, storyboards, wireframes—to test workflow logic early without committing resources to full builds.
quote: low-fidelity mockups can be used to simulate alert-escalation paths or triage workflows, allowing domain experts to walk through hypothetical scenarios

rule: Provide meaningful error messages that include actionable next steps, not just descriptions of what went wrong.
quote: Provide meaningful error messages that include actionable next steps

rule: Place validation error messages near the problematic field and pair with an icon indicator to signal which input needs correction.
quote: Since validation is contextual, it can be helpful to use an icon indicator along with the validation message to help communicate which input(s) are missing or need corrected

rule: Show recently visited pages and items in history lists to help users resume incomplete tasks without recalling details.
quote: Providing access to the pages recently visited and searches performed in the near past can help users resume tasks that they left incomplete and that may have difficulty recalling.

rule: Replace command-line interfaces with visible menus and buttons so users recognize actions rather than recall commands.
quote: A menu system is the most classic example of a recognition-based user interface: the computer shows you the available commands, and you recognize the one you want.

rule: Use contextual tips paired to the current page instead of generic tutorials to help users recognize available actions.
quote: Instead of showing general tutorials, use contextual tips tailored to the page that the user is visiting. Those will allow the user to recognize which actions they may want to do and how.

rule: Tell users what device responses to expect during setup (beeps, blinking lights) so they know the device is responding correctly.
quote: The app should tell users what to expect physically (e.g., beeps or blinking lights), so they know whether the device is responding as expected.

rule: Provide approximate timeframes and explicit status updates during connection to reassure users that processes are ongoing.
quote: Setting expectations with approximate timeframes and instructions (e.g., 'Stay close to your device') helps reassure users that something is happening.

rule: Auto-detect offline devices and automatically notify users with reconnection options rather than leaving them to discover failures.
quote: Automatic triggers. Detect when a device goes offline, automatically notify the user, and offer the option to launch the reconnection wizard, instead of leaving users to figure out if devices are working and how to reconnect them.

rule: Offer error-specific, actionable guidance with quick support links so users troubleshoot without leaving the onboarding flow.
quote: Ideally, errors should also offer built-in support options, so users do not need to abandon the flow to look for help.

rule: Show device status instantly and prominently on the overview screen without navigation so users see all connected devices at a glance.
quote: When users open the app, they should immediately see the status of every connected device, without navigating into individual screens.

rule: Display time remaining or completion percentage during long device tasks so users know progress and trust the device is working.
quote: When a device is performing a task that takes time — whether vacuuming a room, heating water, cooling the house, or running a laundry cycle — users need to know how far along it is.

rule: Store global and local context in separate, dedicated files or databases; keep ambient context in its raw form with API or MCP connections.
quote: Participants generally kept information playing the three roles in separate places. Global and local context lived in distinct files or databases

rule: Enable agents to read and update task-specific context files (local) themselves; document change logs and task lists for the agent to maintain.
quote: Some of it (task lists, change logs, decision logs) is written and kept current by Claude itself, not just read.

rule: Curate global context carefully to relieve users of repeating details across conversations; include best practices, governance rules, brand guidelines, and clarification instructions.
quote: Global context can be powerful because it relieves the user of having to specify these details in each new conversation.

rule: Never delegate editorial judgment or factual verification to AI; humans must always verify flagged claims by returning to original sources.
quote: AI never certifies that the claim is correct. When it flags an issue, it's the editor's or the author's job to go back to the source, double-check the claim

rule: Use AI to identify logical contradictions and structural weaknesses in arguments, but maintain human responsibility for weighing and accepting or rejecting suggestions.
quote: I weigh its suggestions rather than accept them as answers. I keep those that strengthen the argument and that I believe to be applicable, and I discard the rest.

rule: Audit global context in a single sitting; if too long to review at once, move non-universal instructions to local context.
quote: Audit the global context from start to finish once in a while. This context type affects everything the system does, so it should be short enough to review in one sitting.

rule: Name the context type when directing AI to make system changes; retain understanding of impact instead of delegating change comprehension to the AI.
quote: Name the context type when directing a change. Even if users don't know exactly where each file lives or every word inside it, knowing what's happening in each context type allows them to tell the AI, "go update XYZ in the global context" rather than "go fix this wherever you think it matters"

rule: Test filter interactions with real data and user clicks, not static mockups, to discover how the system responds to filtering actions.
quote: a key aspect of filter design is how the system responds when users interact with it (for example, by applying or removing it). To thoroughly test filters, users should be able to click through and use the system as they would with the real product.

rule: Provide AI prototyping tools with detailed prompts describing layout, interactions, edge cases, empty states, and error states to produce high-fidelity results.
quote: Craft a detailed, specific prompt to guide the AI tool in building a high-quality interface. The prompt should describe the interface you want (the layout, the interactions, the edge cases) and include a file containing your data.

rule: Review AI-generated prototypes for design flaws before production: wrong patterns, confusing hierarchy, and unnecessary repetition hide beneath polished appearance.
quote: AI-generated prototypes may look complete while introducing all sorts of assumptions and inaccuracies, such as using the wrong design pattern for the situation, creating a confusing hierarchy, or unnecessarily repeating elements.

rule: Use AI only to organize and summarize research data you've already collected, not to generate user quotes, behaviors, or fill research gaps.
quote: Even though AI should not be used for generating user content in empathy maps, it can be helpful for synthesizing data produced from real-user research.

rule: Frontload key information in the first few words of SMS; users read only the first several words when scanning.
quote: Failing to frontload the key information can cause critical details to be overlooked, as people read only the first several words when scanning a message.

rule: Show individual 'Translate' links only for reviews in languages other than the user's default setting; omit buttons for same-language content.
quote: When sites opt to provide individual translation links like Etsy did, the Translate button should be provided only when the reviews are written in a language other than the default browser setting. In other words, they should not be included on every review.

rule: Allow shoppers to select models by size, height, or skin tone on both product-listing and product-detail pages.
quote: A user shopping for jeans on GoodAmerican.com noticed that she could choose her preferred model early in the shopping journey, on the product-listing page, and again on the product-detail pages.

rule: Persist model selection across all products within a category to reduce interaction cost; do not force users to reselect for each item.
quote: Features that prompt shoppers to select a specific model should persist this selection across all other products within the product category to avoid the interaction cost associated with selecting a model for every product.

rule: Place model-selection buttons or icons in high-contrast, highly visible locations on both category and product pages for discoverability.
quote: Because model-selection features are so valuable to shoppers, they must be easily discoverable and implemented through high-contrast buttons or icons placed in highly visible places on both the category page and the product page.

rule: Consistent application of products and poses across models prevents confusion; ensure the same product shade or fit is clearly applied identically.
quote: Although the page allowed users to view the same shade on different models, the variability in the model poses and in the application of the product, in conjunction with the low visibility of the selected color, made it hard for one shopper to realize what she was viewing.

rule: Integrate livestream into ecommerce apps for informative, detail-oriented sessions; embed livestreams in social-media platforms when entertainment and celebrity influence drive revenue.
quote: If you want your sessions to be informative and detail-oriented, integrate them into ecommerce apps, to supplement your product pages. But if a large portion of your revenue comes from targeted ads on social media or if celebrities play an essential role in promoting your products, embedding livestreams in social-media platforms may be better.
finding: Taobao users (ecommerce app) watched livestreams to gather supplemental product information with a specific shopping goal; Douyin users (social media) treated livestreams as entertainment and made impulsive purchases. Users' mental models of each platform affected whether livestreaming felt relevant.

rule: Segment livestream recommendations by user behavior frequency and interests; show livestreams every 1–2 videos to heavy users and every several minutes to users who dislike livestreams.
quote: The frequency of promoted livestream sessions varied across participants; on average, a livestream session showed up every 3 videos people browsed. But those who enjoy watching livestreams to kill time are shown a livestream promotion for every 1 or 2 videos; in contrast, users who dislike livestreams might browse videos for several minutes without encountering any livestream session.
finding: On Douyin, user interest and behavioral history determined livestream frequency; showing livestreams based on user preference reduced friction and respected browsing patterns.

rule: Define the recurring task before evaluating an AI tool; match the tool's capabilities to that task, not vice versa.
quote: Start with a recurring task that takes meaningful time or effort, then ask whether the tool's capabilities match that task.

rule: Verify that the tool and its data handling comply with your organization's security and privacy policies before use.
quote: Before spending hours testing a tool, make sure it's appropriate for the data you plan to give it. Is the tool approved by your organization?

rule: Benchmark AI output against your own real work samples, not demo results, to assess whether quality is fit for the actual task and its stakes.
quote: Pick an actual example of your own work and ask: is the tool's version better than, as good as, or good enough compared with what you already produce?

rule: Count all time spent on setup, prompting, review, correction, and reformatting when measuring velocity; generation time alone does not predict total time saved.
quote: Compare the total time required with and without the tool: setup, prompting, reviewing, correcting errors, reformatting, and moving material between systems.
finding: A three-second generation can still create a thirty-minute editing job.

rule: Separate one-time friction (setup, learning) from recurring friction (workflow steps, handoffs) when assessing tool fit for ongoing tasks.
quote: It's reasonable for a new tool to require setup and practice, but it's less reasonable for it to lead to an awkward, error-prone workflow forever.

rule: Store research synthesis and design standards in machine-readable formats (e.g., DESIGN.md, UX.md) that AI tools can read when generating anything.
quote: The output of research and design work is, primarily, context that anyone in the organization can include when using AI to generate anything from slides to prototypes to working software.

rule: Keep UX context alongside product code, update it as the product changes, and let AI tools read it on every generation; do not hand it off and leave it behind.
quote: It lives with the product's code, changes when the product changes, and is read by every AI tool in the organization each time something gets generated.

rule: Triage AI-generated features with cost-benefit analysis before refinement; decide what to keep, simplify, integrate, postpone, or remove.
quote: don't start right away by polishing it. Triage it first and do a cost–benefit analysis.

rule: Match evidence rigor to risk level; low-risk features warrant quick tests, high-stakes workflows need rigorous methods.
quote: Match the evidence to the risk involved: a low-risk feature may warrant quick user tests, a new high-stakes workflow may warrant more rigorous (and time-consuming) methods.

rule: Build shared team judgment by explaining triage decisions transparently so teams learn to distinguish buildable from useful features.
quote: Explain why the feature works or doesn't, so the rest of the team learns how to apply the same UX criteria to the next idea.

rule: Capture organizational UX knowledge in context files and design systems to guide AI-generated work and reduce predictable problems.
quote: capture the design and UX knowledge within your organization and use it to inform AI-generated work

rule: Edit AI-generated content ruthlessly to remove messages that obscure core value, redundant controls, and duplicated workflows.
quote: Messages that obscure the core value? Redundant controls? Duplicated workflows? All of these should be removed rather than improved.

rule: Use automation bias safeguards: introduce friction at high-stakes moments and provide easy verification or override methods.
quote: Introducing friction at high-stakes moments and providing easy ways for users to verify or override a result help prevent automation bias.

rule: Ensure human-in-the-loop oversight only works when reviewers have information, time, expertise, and authority to intervene.
quote: it counts as oversight only when the reviewer has the information, time, expertise, and authority to intervene.

rule: Test AI systems with multiple representative inputs run repeatedly; report average performance and confidence intervals, not single outputs.
quote: test multiple representative inputs, run each input repeatedly, and summarize the resulting distribution of scores

rule: Measure both test-input variability and run-to-run variability; identical overall scores can mask different failure patterns.
quote: two customer-service systems are each tested on 10 questions, with 5 runs per question. They both produce acceptable answers on 80% of the 50 runs
finding: Two systems with identical 80% success rates showed different failure distributions: one consistent on supported questions, one unpredictable across all questions.

rule: Document all system details before evaluation: model version, prompts, settings, tools, context, and date; repeat evaluation if any change.
quote: carefully document all the details: record the model and version, prompts or instructions, settings, tools, context, and evaluation date.

rule: Provide critical product details like material, size, and dimensions without jargon; avoid unexplained measurements expecting users to calculate or convert.
quote: At the very least, provide critical product details such as material, size, and heel height.

rule: Show price ranges when exact prices cannot be displayed; all but the wealthiest customers have rough price points in mind.
quote: Consider providing at least a price range when specific prices can't be shown. Remember that all but the wealthiest of customers will have at least a rough price point in mind.

rule: Reserve visual design experimentation for ornamental sections; prioritize readability and function in navigation, filters, descriptions, and payment areas.
quote: perfect places to experiment and let visual design shine without frustrating customers.

rule: Invest in professional copyediting, quality assurance, and translation; typos and bugs damage luxury brand perception more severely than in mainstream ecommerce.
quote: Such sloppy mistakes chipped away at participants' perception of those brands — a disastrous outcome for luxury, where brand reputation is everything.

rule: Include brand history, leadership, and values throughout the site, not only in About Us sections, to foster emotional connections luxury customers seek.
quote: It's a good idea to include interesting company-identity information throughout the site, not just in an About Us section.

rule: During the consideration phase, provide product organization and information architecture that helps users find specific items and categories without friction.
quote: Poor organization and information architecture: Participants struggled to find specific products as well as general product categories.

rule: Explain product names, attributes, and terminology; do not assume luxury shoppers know all brand jargon even if they know the brand well.
quote: Confusing product names, attributes, and terminology: Several sites failed to explain and clarify the different products and their attributes.

rule: Design recommendation systems for digital channels; luxury brand sites often provide no recommendations, unlike in-store where salespeople guide customers.
quote: Bad product recommendations: Unlike the in-store experience, most of these sites provided unhelpful recommendations if at all.

rule: Support generous return policies and address shipping concerns explicitly; anxiety about returns increases with item cost and emotional investment.
quote: Several luxury shoppers also reported feeling anxious about returns.

rule: Explain why a source was searched when its relevance is unclear; show where answers came from, especially when searches span unexpected domains.
quote: When a source's relevance is unclear, explain it, and show where the answer came from.

rule: Format articles clearly; format is the second-largest driver of news site trust, explaining 12% of UX quality.
quote: "Format"—the label for "Articles and other content are formatted in a clear manner"—is the next biggest driver of the news website user experience, explaining 12% of SUPR-Q scores.
finding: Format improvements increase SUPR-Q by 12 percentage points per standardized unit

rule: Include an obvious search bar on news homepages; absent search reduces task completion and frustrates users seeking specific articles.
quote: Neither homepage has an obvious search bar, which users expect to find specific articles.
finding: The Guardian and Huffington Post had lowest task completion rates due to missing visible search functionality

rule: Show category navigation prominently; categories help users find news content and matter more than search alone.
quote: News categories help me find what I am looking for (categories)
finding: Categories ranked as statistically significant driver explaining measurable portion of SUPR-Q scores

rule: Curate homepage selection carefully; good article selection on homepage ranks equally with format as a UX driver.
quote: The homepage contains a good selection of news stories (selection)
finding: Homepage selection explains similar proportion of SUPR-Q as format (approximately 12%)

rule: Display up-to-date content prominently; fewer than half of users believe news sites show current events, damaging loyalty.
quote: Less than half of participants agreed with the statement "The website contains the most up to date current events"
finding: Only 50% or fewer users on most sites felt content was current; Wall Street Journal reached 50% agreement

rule: Return users to their previous scroll position after they visit a product detail page and return to the list.
quote: Always return users to the same place in the list after they visit a product page and then come back

rule: Combine product color or style variants into one list item with interactive swatches; show separate items for variants causes duplicate-listing confusion.
quote: Combine product variations into one listing item rather than showing separate items for each color or style

rule: Use grid layout for visually driven products and list layout for spec-heavy products, or adapt dynamically.
quote: Match the layout to the product type — grid view for visually driven products, list view for spec-heavy products

rule: Protect research phases where learning occurs: moderate sessions live, observe together, debrief as a team, and do interpretive work yourself.
quote: The parts of the process to protect are the ones where the learning lives: moderating sessions, observing them live, debriefing together, and doing the interpretive work of deciding what the data means.

rule: Personal stories trigger wider brain networks than technical content, engaging regions for emotion, memory, and social reasoning more strongly.
quote: Personal narratives triggered a widespread network of activity across listeners, including regions involved in social reasoning, emotional processing, and memory.
finding: Personal narratives engage brain regions associated with emotion, memory, and social reasoning more strongly than nonnarrative text

rule: Reading a comprehensive report creates an illusion of learning; actual retention mirrors students rereading notes without active engagement.
quote: Reading a comprehensive, coherent report can create an 'illusion of learning,' where you feel informed but retain very little afterward.
finding: Perception of preparedness from rereading notes does not correlate with actual performance in long-term-memory tests

rule: Present suggested next steps as easily scannable, clickable buttons rather than buried in lengthy explanations.
quote: Suggested next steps should be easily scannable and self-contained (ideally presented as clickable buttons), rather than buried in lengthy explanations that require careful reading.

rule: Suggest follow-up actions only after the user's primary goal is resolved, not during active task completion.
quote: When a user is working toward a goal, the bot should not distract them with unrelated suggestions. Suggest possible follow-up questions or related topics only after a resolution has been achieved or the primary goal has been addressed.

rule: Close the gap between information and action by linking directly to products, resources, and actions rather than naming them.
quote: Rather than simply naming a product or resource or telling people where to find it, they should link to it directly, including visuals and quick links (e.g., Add to cart , Save to favorites, Compare, Return policy ).

rule: Acknowledge the situation plainly without claiming feelings the bot cannot have; say what happened, not how you feel about it.
quote: When acknowledging users' emotions, a chatbot should not express feelings it cannot have; for example, saying I'm sincerely sorry about the delay can come across as performative. The better approach is to acknowledge the situation — for example, Two weeks is a long time to wait. Let me see what I can do to fix this .

rule: Describe the situation itself, not the user's inner emotional state; avoid claims like 'I understand your disappointment.'
quote: While it's appropriate to describe the situation itself (for example, That's a stressful situation ), chatbots should not make claims about the user's inner state (for example , I understand your disappointment ).

rule: Surface bot capabilities contextually when most relevant, not as an exhaustive opening list that users will forget.
quote: You can outline the bot's scope in its opening message, but don't show an exhaustive list of everything it can do. Users may find that overwhelming and forget it as the conversation moves forward. Instead, surface capabilities contextually , when they are most relevant.

rule: Explain why a limitation exists and what the next step is, not just that you cannot help.
quote: Compare I can't help with that , which is vague, with I don't have access to your purchase history, but I can connect you to someone who does . The second response explains the limitation and the next step.

rule: Make main navigation product hierarchy immediately obvious; hiding catalog behind generic entries like 'Shop' adds friction.
quote: Shoppers should be able to glance at your navigation menu and immediately digest the site's top-level structure

rule: Expose product categories at first navigation level on mobile; hiding them behind generic entry points adds friction.
quote: Hiding your entire catalog behind generic entry points like 'Shop' or 'Products' adds unnecessary friction, especially on mobile where product categories need to be exposed right at the first level

rule: Make size, color, availability, and customization logic immediately clear; users should never decode configuration options.
quote: Users should never have to decode size, color, availability, or customization logic just to figure out if the specific version they want is actually available

rule: Show full order total including shipping, taxes, and fees before checkout; users abandon when costs aren't transparent.
quote: If users can't see a clear order total (including shipping, taxes, and other fees), many will hesitate or abandon rather than start checkout half-informed

rule: Support both increment/decrement buttons and direct text input for quantity; 61% of sites use only one method, creating friction.
quote: 61% of sites in our ecommerce UX benchmark make it unnecessarily difficult for users to update the quantity of cart products, by using either only an open text field or a drop-down, rather than both together
finding: 61% of benchmarked sites use only one quantity edit method instead of both

rule: Offer prominent guest checkout option; 18% of shoppers abandon when forced to create an account.
quote: If users are pushed to sign in or create an account before they can proceed, many interpret it as friction; 18% of shoppers have abandoned a purchase because they were forced to create an account
finding: 18% of shoppers abandon after forced account creation

rule: Design payment fields for typing accuracy with clear validation and alternative payment methods if card isn't standard.
quote: Users need payment fields that support typing accuracy, clear validation, and sensible alternatives if their preferred method isn't standard card entry

rule: Include a review step in multistep checkout so users verify addresses, shipping, payment, and totals before submission.
quote: In multistep checkouts especially, the review step is where users verify addresses, shipping choices, payment details, and totals without having to backtrack through the whole flow

rule: Preserve filter states and cart contents when users move between mobile pages; loss of progress causes context loss.
quote: Users should be able to move back and forth between pages without losing filter states or cart contents

rule: Group mobile page content into collapsed sections to avoid endless scrolling; allow filter refining without excessive tapping.
quote: Users should be able to refine large lists and evaluate product details without opening endless overlays, jumping through tabs, or scrolling through bloated pages

rule: Surface cost, delivery, returns, and stock information early and repeatedly in mobile checkout to prevent late surprises.
quote: Key cost, delivery, returns, and stock information should appear early and repeatedly during the checkout process to help build and maintain purchase confidence

rule: Conduct pre-launch audits of new flows at design stage, not after shipping; fixes cost less and avoid full sprint rework.
quote: A pre-launch audit of a new checkout flow, conducted before development begins, surfaces these issues when they're still design decisions — not engineering changes. The same issue that takes a developer an afternoon to fix in a wireframe can take an entire sprint to fix after it's shipped

rule: Evaluate against external standards to remove internal bias; familiarity blinds teams to first-time user friction.
quote: Familiarity with the website also creates genuine blind spots: interactions that feel intuitive to a team that built them may be confusing to a first-time user

rule: Use research-backed audit standards so findings map to documented failure patterns, not subjective reviewer preference.
quote: A finding isn't rated severe because one reviewer found it annoying. It's rated severe because it maps to a pattern that usability testing has documented as a consistent cause of abandonment or failure

rule: Give mobile UX dedicated audit attention; mobile accounts for ~75% of retail visits but gets late, shallow testing.
quote: Mobile accounts for the majority of ecommerce traffic on most sites, generating around three quarters of retail store visits. Mobile UX is often worse than desktop, and mobile-specific issues are sometimes underrepresented in routine design reviews
finding: Mobile generates ~75% of retail store visits
